After him, they said, there succeeded to the throne a man of Memphis, whose name in the tongue of the Hellenes was Proteus; for whom there is now a sacred enclosure at Memphis, very fair and well ordered, lying on that side of the temple of Hephaestus which faces the North Wind. Round about this enclosure dwell Phoenicians of Tyre, and this whole region is called the Camp of the Tyrians. Within the enclosure of Proteus there is a temple called the temple of the “foreign Aphrodite,” which I conjecture to be one of Helen the daughter of Tyndareus — not only because I have heard the tale how Helen dwelt with Proteus, but also especially because it is called by the name of the “foreign Aphrodite,” for no other temples of Aphrodite elsewhere have the addition of the word “foreign” to the name.

The king of Memphis who held Helen and the stolen treasure in Egypt for the whole length of the Trojan war, and sent Alexander away — the story Herodotus believes over Homer’s.

## modern-en · thonis · 328:0

And the priests told me, when I inquired, that the events concerning Helen happened thus. Alexander, having carried off Helen, was sailing away from Sparta to his own land, and when he had come to the Aegean Sea contrary winds drove him from his course into the Sea of Egypt; and after that, since the blasts did not cease to blow, he came to Egypt itself — and in Egypt to what is now named the Canobic mouth of the Nile and to Taricheiai. Now there was upon the shore, as still there is now, a temple of Heracles, in which if any man's slave takes refuge and has the sacred marks set upon him, giving himself over to the god, it is not lawful to lay hands upon him; and this custom has continued unchanged from the beginning down to my own time. Accordingly, the attendants of Alexander, having heard of the custom that existed about the temple, ran away from him, and sitting down as suppliants of the god, accused Alexander — because they wished to do him harm — telling the whole tale of how things were about Helen and about the wrong done to Menelaus; and they made this accusation not only to the priests but also to the warden of this river-mouth, whose name was Thonis.

The warden of the Canobic mouth who arrested Alexander’s servants and reported him to Proteus.

## modern-en · rhampsinitos · 336:0

After Proteus, they told me, Rhampsinitos succeeded to the kingdom, and he left as his memorial the gateway to the temple of Hephaistos that faces westward. In front of the gateway he set up two statues, each twenty-five cubits tall. The Egyptians call the one on the north side Summer, and the one on the south side Winter; to Summer they pay reverence and make offerings, while to Winter they do the opposite. (a) This king, they said, gained great wealth in silver, more than any king born after him could match or even approach. Wishing to keep his treasure safe, he had a stone chamber built, with one of its walls forming part of the outside of his palace. The builder, however, had a design upon it, and he contrived as follows: he set one of the stones in such a way that it could easily be removed from the wall by two men, or even by a single man. So when the chamber was finished and the king stored his money inside it, the builder, after some time, drawing near the end of his life, called his two sons to him. He told them how he had arranged the matter when building the king's treasury, all in forethought for them, so that they might have ample means of living. He gave them the precise measurements for removing the stone, telling them that if they paid heed to this, they would be the stewards of the king's treasury. Then he died, and his sons made no long delay in setting to work. They went to the palace by night, found the stone in the wall of the chamber, dealt with it easily, and carried away a great quantity of the wealth within. (b) When the king happened to open the chamber, he was astonished to see the vessels falling short of their full amount, and he did not know whom to blame, since the seals were unbroken and the chamber had been shut close. But when, on opening the chamber a second time and a third, the money was each time seen to be diminished — for the thieves did not slacken in their assaults — he did as follows. He had traps made and set them around the vessels in which the money was kept; and when the thieves came as before and one of them entered, as soon as he came near a vessel he was caught fast in the trap. Realizing how desperate his case was, he immediately called his brother, showed him what had happened, and bade him climb in as quickly as possible and cut off his head, lest he be seen and recognized, bringing destruction upon his brother as well. To the other this seemed sound advice, and he was persuaded; he did so, and fitting the stone back into its place, he departed home carrying his brother's head with him. (c) When day came, the king entered the chamber and was utterly amazed to see the body of the thief held in the trap without its head, the chamber unbroken, and no way to come in or go out. Being at a loss, he hung the dead body up on the wall and set guards there, with orders to seize anyone seen weeping or lamenting and bring him before the king. When the body had been hung up, the mother was deeply grieved. Speaking with her surviving son, she ordered him to contrive, by whatever means he could, to take down and bring home the body of his dead brother; and if he failed to do this, she earnestly threatened that she would go and inform the king that he had the money. (d) Since the mother dealt harshly with the surviving son, and he could not persuade her with his many arguments, he contrived a device for his purpose. He provided himself with asses, filled some skins with wine, loaded them upon the asses, and drove them along. When he came opposite to those guarding the corpse, he pulled out two or three of the necks of the skins and loosened the cords with which they were tied. As the wine ran out, he began to beat his head and cry out loudly, as if he did not know which of the asses to turn to first. When the guards saw the wine flowing out in streams, they ran together onto the road with drinking vessels in their hands and collected the wine that was spilling, counting it pure gain. He railed at them all violently, pretending to be angry, and when the guards tried to appease him, after a while he feigned to be pacified and to abate his anger. At last he drove his asses out of the road and began to set their loads right. Then more talk arose among them, one or two of them made jokes at him and brought him to laugh with them, and in the end he made them a present of one of the skins as well. At that they lay down then and there without further ado, intending to drink, and they took him into their company and invited him to stay with them and join them in their drinking. So he, as one might expect, was persuaded and stayed. As they welcomed him in friendly fashion as they drank, he made them a present of another skin. So at length, having drunk liberally, the guards became completely drunk, and being overcome by sleep they went to bed on the very spot where they had been drinking. He then, since it was now far on in the night, first took down the body of his brother, and then in mockery shaved the right cheeks of all the guards. After that he placed the dead body upon the asses and drove them home, having accomplished what his mother had enjoined upon him. (e) When it was reported to the king that the dead body of the thief had been stolen away, he displayed great anger; and desiring above all to find out who it could be that devised these things, he did this — so at least they said, though I do not believe the account. He caused his own daughter to sit in a brothel and ordered her to receive all comers equally, and before lying with any of them she was to compel each one to tell her what was the most cunning and the most unholy deed he had done in all his life; and whoever should relate what had happened concerning the thief, she must seize him and not let him go. So she did as her father had enjoined. The thief, hearing the purpose for which this was done and wishing to outdo the king in cleverness, did this. From the body of one lately dead he cut off the arm at the shoulder and went with it under his cloak. Having gone in to the king's daughter and being asked the same question as the others, he related that he had done the most unholy deed when he cut off the head of his brother caught in a trap in the king's treasure-chamber, and the most cunning deed when he made the guards drunk and took down the dead body of his brother that had been hung up. When she heard this and tried to lay hold of him, the thief held out to her in the darkness the arm of the corpse, which she grasped and held, thinking she was holding the man's own arm. But the thief left it in her hands and departed, escaping through the door. (f) When this also was reported to the king, he was at first amazed at the ready invention and daring of the fellow. Then afterwards he sent round to all the cities and made proclamation, granting a free pardon to the thief and promising a great reward as well if he would come into his presence. The thief, trusting to the proclamation, came to the king, and Rhampsinitos marvelled greatly at him and gave him this daughter of his to wife, considering him to be the most knowing of all men. For just as the Egyptians were distinguished from all other men, so was he distinguished from the other Egyptians.

The rich king whose treasury a mason’s two sons robbed through a movable stone — the best story in Book 2 — and who ended by marrying his daughter to the thief.

## modern-en · cheops · 339:0

Down to the time when Rhampsinitos was king, they told me, there was nothing in Egypt but orderly rule, and Egypt prospered greatly. But after him Cheops became king and brought them to every kind of misery. He shut up all the temples, and having first stopped them from sacrificing there, he then ordered all the Egyptians to work for him. Some were assigned to drag stones from the quarries in the Arabian mountains to the Nile; others he ordered to receive the stones after they had been ferried across the river in boats, and to haul them to the so-called Libyan mountains. They worked in shifts of a hundred thousand men at a time, for three months straight. Ten years of this oppression passed while the causeway was built along which they hauled the stones — a causeway that is, in my view, a work not much less than the pyramid itself. Its length is five furlongs, its breadth ten fathoms, and its height, where it is highest, eight fathoms, and it is made of smoothed stone with figures carved upon it. For this, they said, the ten years were spent, as well as for the underground chambers on the hill on which the pyramids stand, which he had made as burial chambers for himself on an island, having led a channel from the Nile to the place. For the construction of the pyramid itself a period of twenty years passed. The pyramid is square, each side measuring eight hundred feet, and its height is the same. It is built of smoothed stones fitted together in the most perfect manner, not one of the stones being less than thirty feet in length.

The king who shut the temples, set the whole people to work on his pyramid for twenty years, and sold his own daughter’s favours to pay for it.

## modern-en · chephren · 342:0

This Cheops, the Egyptians said, reigned for fifty years; and after he died, his brother Chephren succeeded to the kingdom. This king followed the same pattern as the other in every respect, including the fact that he built a pyramid. His pyramid did not reach the dimensions of the one built by his predecessor — I know this, having measured it myself — and moreover it has no underground chambers beneath it, nor does a channel from the Nile flow to it as to the other, where the water coming through a built conduit flows around an island within, and where they say Cheops himself is buried. But for a foundation he laid the first course in Ethiopian stone of varied colors. He built this pyramid forty feet lower than the other in size, placing it next to the great pyramid. The two stand on the same hill, which is about a hundred feet high. And Chephren, they said, reigned fifty-six years.

Cheops’s brother and successor, who ruled in the same manner for fifty-six years; the Egyptians will not willingly say either brother’s name.

## modern-en · mykerinos · 344:0

After him, they said, Mykerinos became king over Egypt — the son of Cheops. His father's deeds displeased him, and he both opened the temples and gave the people, who had been ground down to the last extremity of misery, their liberty to return to their own affairs and to their sacrifices. He also handed down judgments in their lawsuits that were more just than those of all the other kings. For this reason the Egyptians praise this king above all the kings who had arisen in Egypt before him; for he not only gave good decisions, but also, when a man complained of a decision, he paid him compensation out of his own property and so satisfied his desire. But while Mykerinos was acting mercifully to his subjects and conducting himself in the way I have described, calamities befell him. The first was this: his daughter died, the only child he had in his house. Grieved beyond measure by what had happened, and wishing to bury his daughter in a more remarkable manner than others, he made a cow of wood, covered it over with gold, and then buried within it this daughter who, as I said, had died.

Cheops’s son, who opened the temples again and gave the people back their lives — and was told by the oracle that he had six years to live because Egypt was meant to suffer a hundred and fifty. He answered by lighting lamps and living the nights as well.

## modern-en · asychis · 351:0

After Mykerinos, the priests said, Asychis became king of Egypt, and he built for Hephaistos the temple gateway that faces the sunrise — by far the most beautiful and largest of the gateways. While all of them have figures carved upon them and countless other architectural ornaments, this one has them far more than the rest. In this king's reign, they told me, as the circulation of money was very slow, a law was passed for the Egyptians allowing a man to borrow the money he needed by offering as security the dead body of his father. An additional clause was added: the lender was to have a claim on the whole burial chamber belonging to the borrower, and the borrower who offered this security, if he refused to repay the debt, would be subject to this penalty — that neither he himself would be allowed burial when he died, either in the family tomb or any other, nor would he be allowed to bury any kinsman who died. Wishing to surpass the kings of Egypt before him, this king left as his memorial a pyramid that he made of bricks, on which there is an inscription carved in stone that says: “Do not despise me in comparison with the pyramids of stone, for I surpass them as much as Zeus surpasses the other gods. For with a pole they struck into the lake, and whatever mud stuck to the pole, they gathered up and made into bricks, and in this way they finished me.”

The king who made a law that a man might borrow on his father’s corpse, and built a pyramid of brick with an inscription telling it not to compare itself with the stone ones.

## modern-en · sethos · 356:0

After him the priest of Hephaistos, whose name was Sethos, came to the throne. This man, they said, neglected and held in no regard the warrior class of the Egyptians, thinking he would have no need of them. Besides other slights he put upon them, he also took from them the plots of grain-land which had been granted to them as a special gift in the reigns of previous kings — twelve plots to each man. After this, Sanacharib, king of the Arabians and Assyrians, marched a great army against Egypt. Then the warriors of the Egyptians refused to come to the rescue, and the priest, being driven into a tight corner, entered the sanctuary of the temple and lamented before the image of the god the danger hanging over him. As he was lamenting, sleep came over him, and in his vision it seemed that the god came and stood beside him and encouraged him, saying he would suffer no harm if he went out to meet the army of the Arabians, for he himself would send him helpers. Trusting in what he had seen in his sleep, he took with him, they said, those Egyptians who were willing to follow, and encamped at Pelusion, for that was the route of the invasion. Not one of the warrior class followed him, but shopkeepers, artisans, and men of the marketplace. Then, after they arrived, field mice swarmed by night upon their enemies and ate through their quivers and their bows, and moreover the handgrips of their shields, so that the next day they fled, and being without weapons to defend themselves, great numbers of them fell. To this day this king stands in the temple of Hephaistos in stone, holding a mouse on his hand, and by letters inscribed he says these words: “Let whoever looks upon me learn to fear the gods.”

The priest of Hephaistos who despised the warrior class and was saved from Sennacherib by field-mice that ate the Assyrians’ bowstrings overnight.

## modern-en · psammetichos · 104:0

From there they went on to invade Egypt; and when they were in Syria, which is called Palestine, Psammetichus, king of Egypt, met them, and by gifts and entreaties he turned them from their purpose so that they should advance no further. As they retreated, when they came to the city of Ascalon in Syria, most of the Scythians passed through without doing any damage, but a few of them who had stayed behind plundered the temple of Aphrodite Urania. This temple, as I find by inquiry, is the most ancient of all the temples that belong to this goddess; for the temple in Cyprus was founded from this one, as the people of Cyprus themselves report, and it was the Phoenicians who founded the temple in Cythera, coming from this land of Syria. So these Scythians who had plundered the temple at Ascalon, and their descendants forever after, were smitten by the divinity with a disease that made them women instead of men. The Scythians say that for this reason they were diseased, and that for this reason travelers who visit Scythia today see among them the affliction of those whom the Scythians call Enareis.

One of the twelve kings, driven out and returned with the bronze men the oracle promised; he reunited Egypt, opened it to Greek traders, and shut two children away with a mute shepherd to find out which language came first. The two editions spell him Psammetichos and Psammetichus.

## modern-en · necos · 367:0

This Psammetichos had previously been a fugitive from the Ethiopian Sabacos, who had killed his father Necos; from him, I say, he had been a fugitive in Syria. When the Ethiopian departed as a result of the vision in the dream, the Egyptians of the district of Saïs brought him back to his own country. Afterwards, when he was king, it was his fate to be a fugitive a second time on account of the helmet, being driven by the eleven kings into the marshland. Holding that he had been gravely wronged by them, he considered how he might take vengeance on those who had driven him out. When he sent to the oracle of Leto in the city of Buto, where the Egyptians have their most truthful oracle, he was given the reply that vengeance would come when men of bronze appeared from the sea. He was strongly inclined not to believe that bronze men would come to help him; but not long afterwards, certain Ionians and Carians who had sailed out for plunder were forced to come ashore in Egypt, and having landed and being clad in bronze armor, one of the Egyptians, never having seen men in bronze armor before, came to the marshland and brought word to Psammetichos that bronze men had come from the sea and were plundering the plain. He, perceiving that the saying of the oracle was coming to pass, dealt in a friendly manner with the Ionians and Carians, and with large promises persuaded them to take his side. Then, having persuaded them, with the help of the Egyptians who favored his cause and of these foreign mercenaries, he overthrew the kings.

When Psammis had been king of Egypt for only six years and had made an expedition to Ethiopia, and immediately afterwards ended his life, Apries son of Psammis inherited the kingdom in succession. This man came to be the most prosperous of all the kings up to that time, except only his forefather Psammetichos, and he reigned twenty-five years, during which he led an army against Sidon and fought a sea-battle with the king of Tyre. Indignant at this, both the men who had returned from the expedition and the friends of those who had perished openly revolted.

To Amasis what was done was not entirely unwelcome, as he showed by his behavior; for as soon as the rebellious Egyptians had set him up as king, he prepared to march against Apries. Apries, hearing this, sent one of his own attendants to Amasis, a man of reputation whose name was Patarbemis, ordering him to bring Amasis alive into his presence. When Patarbemis came and summoned Amasis, the latter, who happened to be sitting on horseback, lifted up his leg and behaved in an unseemly manner, telling him to take that back to Apries. Nevertheless, they say, Patarbemis pressed him to go to the king, since the king had sent to summon him, and he replied that for some time past he had been preparing to do so, and that Apries would have no cause to fault him. Then Patarbemis, perceiving his intent both from what he said and from seeing his preparations, departed in haste, wishing to inform the king as quickly as possible of what was going on. ## modern-en · ladice · 396:0

Amasis also made a pact of friendship and alliance with the people of Cyrene. He decided to take a wife from there—either because he wanted a Greek wife, or simply out of friendship for Cyrene. He married a woman named Ladice, said by some to be the daughter of Battus, by others of Arcesilaus, and by still others of Critobulos, a prominent citizen. When Amasis lay with her, he found himself unable to consummate the marriage, though he had no trouble with his other wives. After this continued for some time, Amasis told Ladice he believed she had used witchcraft on him, and that nothing could save her from the worst death of any woman. Ladice denied everything, but Amasis was unmoved. So she silently vowed to Aphrodite that if Amasis lay with her successfully that night, she would send a statue to the goddess at Cyrene. Immediately after the vow, Amasis was able to perform. From then on, every time he came to her, he succeeded. He loved her very much after that. Ladice fulfilled her vow and sent the statue, which was still in good condition in my time, set up facing outward from the city of Cyrene. When Cambyses conquered Egypt and learned who Ladice was, he sent her home to Cyrene unharmed.

The Cyrenaean woman Amasis married, who prayed to Aphrodite when he could not come to her and afterwards sent the goddess a statue.

This pyramid some of the Greeks claim was built by the courtesan Rhodopis, but in saying this they are not speaking correctly. Besides, it is obvious to me that those who say this do not even know who Rhodopis was — otherwise they would not have attributed to her the building of a pyramid like this, on which, so to speak, countless thousands of talents were spent. By descent she was Thracian, and she was a slave of Iadmon son of Hephaistopolis, a Samian, and a fellow-slave of Aesop the fable-maker — for he too was once the slave of Iadmon, as was proved especially by this fact: when the people of Delphi repeatedly proclaimed, in accordance with an oracle, that someone should claim the blood-money for Aesop's death, no one else came forward, but at length the grandson of Iadmon, also called Iadmon, claimed it; and so it is shown that Aesop too was Iadmon's slave.

By descent she was Thracian, and she was a slave of Iadmon son of Hephaistopolis, a Samian, and a fellow-slave of Aesop the fable-maker — for he too was once the slave of Iadmon, as was proved especially by this fact: when the people of Delphi repeatedly proclaimed, in accordance with an oracle, that someone should claim the blood-money for Aesop's death, no one else came forward, but at length the grandson of Iadmon, also called Iadmon, claimed it; and so it is shown that Aesop too was Iadmon's slave.

## modern-en · charaxos · 350:0

As for Rhodopis, she came to Egypt brought by Xanthes the Samian, and having arrived there to practice her trade, she was ransomed from slavery for a large sum by a man of Mytilene, Charaxos son of Scamandronymos, the brother of Sappho the lyric poet. Thus Rhodopis was set free, and she remained in Egypt, and by her beauty she won so much favor that she made a great deal of money — great for someone like Rhodopis — though not enough to cover the cost of such a pyramid as this. In fact, there is no need to credit her with very great wealth, since the tithe of her wealth can still be seen even now by anyone who wants to look. For Rhodopis wished to leave behind in Hellas a memorial of herself — something that no one else had thought of or dedicated in a temple — and to offer it at Delphi as her memorial. Accordingly, with the tithe of her wealth she had iron spits made, large enough to pierce a whole ox, and many in number, going as far as her tithe allowed. She sent them to Delphi, and they are still lying there today, heaped together behind the altar the Chians dedicated, directly opposite the inner sanctum of the temple. As it happens, the courtesans at Naucratis tend to win renown, for this woman first, about whom this story is told, became so famous that every Greek without exception came to know the name of Rhodopis; and after her, one named Archidiche was sung about throughout Hellas, though she was less talked about than the former. As for Charaxos, after ransoming Rhodopis and returning to Mytilene, he was savagely abused by Sappho in an ode. About Rhodopis, then, I will say no more.

For in the parts of Libya along the Northern Sea, beginning from Egypt and going as far as the headland of Soloeis (which is the extreme point of Libya), Libyans — and many races of them — extend along the whole coast, except such portions as the Hellenes and Phoenicians hold. But in the upper parts, which lie above the seacoast and above the peoples whose land comes down to the sea, Libya is full of wild beasts; and in the parts beyond the land of wild beasts it is full of sand, terribly waterless, and utterly desert. These young men then (they said), being sent out by their companions well supplied with water and provisions, went first through the inhabited country; after they had passed through this, they came to the country of wild beasts; and after this they passed through the desert, making their way towards the West Wind. Neither could the Nasamonians understand anything of their speech nor could those who were carrying them off understand the speech of the Nasamonians; and they led them (so it is said) through very great swamps, and after passing through these they came to a city in which all the men were of the same short stature as those who had carried them off, and black of skin. When the historian Hecataeus visited Thebes and traced his ancestry back to a god in the sixteenth generation, the priests of Zeus did much the same for him as they did for me (though I did not trace my own genealogy). They traced their counter-genealogy like this: each statue, they said, was a piromis born of a piromis (meaning a good and noble man). And even supposing that for the first part of the time they had been so inclined, yet when many other Trojans besides were losing their lives as often as they fought with the Hellenes, and when of Priam's own sons two or three or even more were slain in every battle (if one may trust at all the Epic poets) — when, I say, things were coming to such a pass, I believe that even if Priam himself had had Helen as wife, he would have given her back to the Achaeans, if by so doing he might be freed from the evils that oppressed him. Nor was the kingdom coming to Alexander next, so that with Priam old the government was in his hands; but Hector, who was both older and more of a man than he, would have received it after Priam's death, and it would not have befitted Hector to allow his brother to continue his wrongdoing, seeing that great evils were coming to pass on his account both to himself privately and in general to the other Trojans. In truth, however, they lacked the power to give Helen back; and the Hellenes did not believe them, though they spoke the truth — because, as I declare my opinion, the divine power was purposing to cause them utterly to perish, and so make it evident to men that for great wrongs great also are the chastisements that come from the gods. So they say, and they honour Perseus in Hellenic fashion thus: they hold an athletic contest, which includes the whole list of games, and they offer as prizes cattle, cloaks, and skins. When I asked why Perseus appeared to them alone, and why they were separated from all the other Egyptians in holding an athletic contest, they said that Perseus had been born of their city; for Danaus and Lynceus, they said, were men of Chemmis and had sailed to Hellas, and from them they traced a descent down to Perseus. They told me he had come to Egypt for the reason the Hellenes also give — namely to bring the Gorgon's head from Libya — and had then visited them too and recognised all his kinsfolk; and they said he had thoroughly learnt the name of Chemmis before coming to Egypt, since he had heard it from his mother, and that they celebrated an athletic contest for him by his own command.

About Heracles I heard the account that he was one of the twelve gods; but of the other Heracles whom the Hellenes know I was not able to hear anything in any part of Egypt. Moreover, to prove that the Egyptians did not take the name of Heracles from the Hellenes, but rather the Hellenes from the Egyptians — I mean those of the Hellenes who gave the name Heracles to the son of Amphitryon — of this, besides many other proofs, there is chiefly this: that the parents of this Heracles, Amphitryon and Alcmene, were both of Egyptian descent; and also that the Egyptians say they know neither the name of Poseidon nor of the Dioscuri, nor have these been accepted by them as gods among their other gods. Yet if they had received the name of any divinity from the Hellenes, they would naturally have preserved the memory of these most of all — assuming, as I suppose and as my judgment compels me to think, that in those times, as now, some of the Hellenes made voyages and were seafaring folk; so that the Egyptians would have learnt the names of these gods even more than that of Heracles. In fact, however, Heracles is a very ancient Egyptian god; and (as the Egyptians themselves say) it is seventeen thousand years to the beginning of the reign of Amasis from the time when the twelve gods — of whom they count Heracles one — were begotten of the eight gods.

Heracles’s mortal father — of Egyptian descent, the Egyptians say, which is why the Greeks are wrong about which Heracles is older.

Now I think that Melampus the son of Amytheon was not without knowledge of these rites of sacrifice, but was acquainted with them. For Melampus is the one who first set forth to the Hellenes the name of Dionysus and the manner of sacrifice and the procession of the phallos. Strictly speaking, when he made it known he did not take in the whole of it; but those wise men who came after him made it known more at large. Melampus, then, is the one who taught about the phallos that is carried in procession for Dionysus; and from him the Hellenes learnt to do what they do. I say, then, that Melampus, being a man of ability, devised for himself an art of divination, and having learnt from Egypt he taught the Hellenes many things, and among them those that concern Dionysus, making changes in some few points of them. For I shall not say that what is done in the worship of the god in Egypt came accidentally to be the same as what is done among the Hellenes, for then these rites would have been in character with the Hellenic worship and not lately brought in; nor indeed shall I say that the Egyptians took either this or any other customary observance from the Hellenes. But I think it most probable that Melampus learnt the matters concerning Dionysus from Cadmus the Tyrian and from those who came with him from Phoenicia to the land we now call Boeotia.

Son of Amytheon, who Herodotus thinks brought the rite of Dionysus into Greece from Egypt, having learned it from Cadmus and the Phoenicians.

For this reason no Egyptian man or woman would kiss a Hellene on the mouth, nor will they use a knife, roasting-spits, or cauldron belonging to a Hellene, nor taste of the flesh even of a clean animal if it has been cut with a Hellene's knife. They bury the cattle of this kind that die in the following manner. The females they throw into the river, but the males they bury, each people in the outskirts of their town, with one of the horns (or sometimes both) protruding to mark the place. When the bodies have rotted away and the appointed time comes, then to each city comes a boat from what is called the island of Prosopitis (this is in the Delta, and the circuit of it measures nine schoeni). On this island of Prosopitis, besides many other cities, stands the one from which the boats come to collect the bones of the oxen; the city's name is Atarbechis, and in it there is a holy temple of Aphrodite. From this city many go out in various directions, some to one city and some to another, and when they have dug up the bones of the oxen they carry them off, and all together they bury them in a single place. In the same way they bury their other cattle when these die, for the same law is laid down concerning them, and these too they abstain from killing.

How then should it flow from snow, when it flows from the hottest parts to those which are cooler? Indeed most of the facts are such as to convince any reasoning man that it is not at all likely it flows from snow. The first and greatest evidence is the winds, which blow hot from these regions; the second is that the land there is always rainless and without frost, whereas after snow has fallen rain must necessarily come within five days, so that if it snowed in those parts rain would fall there; the third evidence is the people dwelling there, who are black in colour because of the burning heat. Moreover, kites and swallows remain there throughout the year and do not leave the land; and cranes, fleeing the cold that sets in over Scythia, come regularly to these parts to winter. For in the parts of Libya along the Northern Sea, beginning from Egypt and going as far as the headland of Soloeis (which is the extreme point of Libya), Libyans — and many races of them — extend along the whole coast, except such portions as the Hellenes and Phoenicians hold. But in the upper parts, which lie above the seacoast and above the peoples whose land comes down to the sea, Libya is full of wild beasts; and in the parts beyond the land of wild beasts it is full of sand, terribly waterless, and utterly desert. These young men then (they said), being sent out by their companions well supplied with water and provisions, went first through the inhabited country; after they had passed through this, they came to the country of wild beasts; and after this they passed through the desert, making their way towards the West Wind. But as they began to pluck it, small men came upon them — of less stature than men of the common size — and these seized them and carried them off. Neither could the Nasamonians understand anything of their speech nor could those who were carrying them off understand the speech of the Nasamonians; and they led them (so it is said) through very great swamps, and after passing through these they came to a city in which all the men were of the same short stature as those who had carried them off, and black of skin. By the city ran a great river, which flowed from the west toward the sunrise, and in it were seen crocodiles.

This man rose against him, realizing that the death of Smerdis was being kept secret, that only a few of the Persians knew of it, while the greater number believed without doubt that he was still alive. He therefore tried to seize the kingdom, and he formed his plan as follows. He had a brother—the one who, as I said, rose with him against Cambyses—and this man very closely resembled in appearance Smerdis son of Cyrus, whom Cambyses had killed, his own brother. He resembled Smerdis in form, and not only so, but he had the same name, Smerdis. Having persuaded this man that he would manage everything for him, the Magian Patizeithes brought him and seated him on the royal throne. Then he sent heralds to the various provinces, and among them one to the army in Egypt, to proclaim that from now on they were to obey Smerdis son of Cyrus instead of Cambyses.

The brother left in charge of Cambyses’s household, who seized the throne because he knew the real Smerdis was dead and that almost nobody else did. He was his namesake, and he reigned seven months and did his subjects good; the Persians killed him when Otanes found out, through his own daughter, that the man in the bed had no ears.

It was against this Amasis that Cambyses son of Cyrus was making his expedition, taking with him not only the other peoples over whom he ruled but also Greeks, both Ionians and Aiolians; and the cause of the expedition was as follows. Amasis, vexed and afraid of the power of the Persians, knew neither how to give nor how to refuse, for he was well aware that Cambyses meant to keep her not as a wife but as a concubine. Reckoning it this way, he did the following: there was a daughter of the former king Apries, very tall and of comely form, the only surviving member of his house, and her name was Nitetis. But after a time, when Cambyses greeted her, calling her by the name of her father, the girl said to him: “O king, you do not realize how you have been deceived by Amasis; for he dressed me up in finery and sent me off, giving me to you as his own daughter, whereas in truth I am the daughter of Apries, against whom Amasis rose up along with the Egyptians and murdered him, though he was his lord and master.” These words, and the occasion that produced them, led Cambyses son of Cyrus against Egypt, moved to very great anger.

Meanwhile, Psammenitos the son of Amasis was camped at the Pelusian mouth of the Nile, waiting for Cambyses. Cambyses did not find Amasis alive when he invaded Egypt. I was witness, moreover, to a great marvel, which the local inhabitants pointed out to me. Of the bones scattered about of those who fell in this fight — each side lying separately, since the bones of the Persians were heaped on one side, where they had been laid apart at the start, and those of the Egyptians on the other — the skulls of the Persians are so weak that if you hit them with just a pebble you will make a hole in them, while those of the Egyptians are so exceedingly strong that you would hardly break them by striking them with a large stone. The cause of this, they said — and I for my part readily believe them — is that the Egyptians from early childhood shave their heads, and the bone is thickened by exposure to the sun. This is also the reason why they do not become bald: for among the Egyptians you see fewer bald-headed men than among any other race. This, then, is why they have strong skulls. The reason the Persians have weak ones is that from infancy they keep their heads delicately in the shade by wearing tiaras, that is, felt caps. So much for that. I saw a similar thing at Papremis in the case of those who were slain along with Achaimenes son of Dareios, by Inaros the Libyan.

Now while Cambyses was marching against Egypt, the Lacedemonians had also made an expedition against Samos and against Polycrates son of Aiakes, who had risen up against the government and gained power over Samos. At first he had divided the state into three parts and given a share to his brothers Pantagnotos and Syloson; but afterwards he put one of them to death, and drove out the younger, Syloson, and so obtained possession of all Samos. Then, being in possession, he made a guest-friendship with Amasis king of Egypt, sending him gifts and receiving gifts in return. After this, within a short period, the power of Polycrates increased rapidly, and there was much fame of it not only in Ionia but also over the rest of Hellas: for wherever he directed his forces, everything went fortunately for him. He had gotten for himself a hundred fifty-oared galleys and a thousand archers, and he plundered all men indiscriminately, making no distinction; for he used to say that he would earn more gratitude from a friend by giving back what he had taken than by not taking at all. So he had conquered many of the islands and many cities on the mainland, and besides other things he won a sea-fight against the Lesbians as they were coming with their forces to aid the Milesians, and defeated them; and these men dug the whole trench round the wall of the city of Samos while working in chains.

Polycrates’s brother, exiled — and the man who gave Darius a red cloak in Egypt for nothing, years before Darius was king, and afterwards asked for Samos and got it.

## modern-en · eupalinos · 457:0

I have spoken at some length about the Samians because they have three works that are greater than any others ever constructed by Hellenes. First, a tunnel, open at both ends, dug through a mountain no less than one hundred and fifty fathoms high. The tunnel is seven furlongs long and eight feet high and wide, and throughout its whole length another channel has been cut twenty cubits deep and three feet wide, through which water is piped to the city from an abundant spring. The designer of this work was a Megarian, Eupalinos son of Naustrophos. That is one of the three. The second is a mole in the sea around the harbour, reaching down as much as twenty fathoms; its length is more than two furlongs. The third work they have accomplished is a temple larger than any other temple we know of. Its first designer was Rhoicos son of Philes, a native of Samos. For these reasons I have spoken at greater length of the Samians.

The Megarian engineer of the Samian tunnel, seven furlongs through a mountain and open at both ends — the first of the three greatest Greek works Herodotus knows.

Now about the time of Cambyses' illness, this had come to pass. There was a certain Oroetes, a Persian, whom Cyrus had appointed governor of the province of Sardis. This man had set his heart on an unholy thing. Though he had never suffered any wrong from Polycrates the Samian, nor heard a single offensive word from him, nor even seen him, he desired to seize him and put him to death, for a reason of this kind, as most who tell the story say. While Oroetes and another Persian named Mitrobates, governor of the province of Daskyleion, were sitting at the door of the king's court, they passed from words to a quarrel. As they disputed their respective claims to distinction, Mitrobates taunted Oroetes and said: “Do you count yourself a man? You have never yet won the island of Samos for the king, though it lies close to your province and is so extraordinarily easy to take that a native of it rose up against the government with fifteen men-at-arms, seized the island, and is now its despot.” Some say that because he heard this and was stung by the reproach, he conceived the desire not so much to take vengeance on the man who said it, as to destroy Polycrates at all costs, since it was on account of him that he was spoken of ill.

The Persian governor of Sardis who had Polycrates crucified out of nothing but pique at a slight he had imagined, and murdered Mitrobates and his son as well. Darius had him killed by a letter read out to his own guards.

## modern-en · bagaios · 525:0

Thus Darius asked, and thirty men undertook the task, each eager to do it himself. Darius stopped their contention and bade them cast lots. When they did so, Bagaios son of Artontes drew the lot out of them all. Having drawn the lot, Bagaios acted as follows: he wrote many papers dealing with various matters and set Darius' seal on them, and with these he went to Sardis. When he arrived there and came into Oroetes' presence, he took the covers off the papers one by one and gave them to the Royal Secretary to read—for all provincial governors have Royal Secretaries. Now Bagaios gave the papers in order to test the spearmen of the guard, to see whether they would accept the idea of revolting from Oroetes. When he saw that they paid great reverence to the papers and still greater reverence to the words read from them, he handed over another paper containing these words: “Persians, King Darius forbids you to serve as guards to Oroetes.” Hearing this, they lowered the points of their spears before him. Then Bagaios, seeing that they were obedient to the paper on this point, took courage and gave the last paper to the secretary. In it was written: “King Darius commands the Persians in Sardis to kill Oroetes.” So the spearmen of the guard, when they heard this, drew their swords and killed him on the spot. Thus retribution for the murder of Polycrates the Samian overtook Oroetes.

The son of Artontes who drew the lot, went to Sardis with a bundle of letters, and had Oroetes’s own bodyguard kill him by reading the last one aloud.

Now Periander had chosen out the sons of the leading men of Corcyra and was sending them to Sardis to be made eunuchs in order to take his revenge, since the Corcyreans had first begun the offense and had done him a deed of reckless wrong. For after Periander had killed his wife Melissa, it happened to him to experience another misfortune in addition to what had already happened, and it was this. He had by Melissa two sons, one seventeen and the other eighteen years old. Their mother's father Procles, who was despot of Epidauros, sent for these sons to visit him and entertained them kindly, as might be expected since they were the sons of his own daughter. When he was sending them back, he said in taking leave of them: “Boys, do you know who killed your mother?” The elder of the two took no notice of this saying, but the younger, whose name was Lycophron, was so greatly grieved at hearing it that when he returned to Corinth, he would neither address his father, nor speak to him when his father tried to converse with him, nor give any reply when asked questions, regarding him as the murderer of his mother. At length Periander, enraged with his son, drove him out of his house.

Periander’s wife, whom he killed, and whose ghost would not name the hiding-place of a deposit until he had burnt real clothes for her in the pit at Corinth.

The Corinthians also took part zealously in this expedition against Samos, so that it might be carried out; for an offense had been committed against them as well by the Samians, a generation before this expedition and around the same time as the robbery of the bowl. Periander son of Kypselos had dispatched three hundred sons of the leading men of Corcyra to Alyattes at Sardis to be made eunuchs; and when the Corinthians escorting the boys put in at Samos, the Samians, having learned the story and for what purpose the boys were being conducted to Sardis, first instructed the boys to seize the temple of Artemis, and then refused to permit the Corinthians to drag the suppliants away from the temple. And when the Corinthians cut the boys off from supplies of food, the Samians made a festival, which they celebrate in the same manner to this day. For when night came on, as long as the boys were suppliants, they arranged dances of maidens and youths, and in arranging the dances they made it a rule of the festival that sweet cakes of sesame and honey should be carried, so that the Corcyrean boys might snatch them and so have sustenance. This went on for so long that at last the Corinthians who had charge of the boys departed and went away; and the Samians carried the boys back to Corcyra.

Periander’s enemies, who killed his son to keep him out and whose three hundred boys he sent to Sardis to be made eunuchs; the Samians saved them.

The Samians who had gone on the expedition against Polycrates also sailed away when the Lacedaemonians were about to abandon them, and came to Siphnos. They were short of money, and the Siphnians at that time were at the peak of their prosperity and had more wealth than any of the other islanders, since they had mines of gold and silver on their island. So rich were these mines that there is a treasury dedicated at Delphi from the tithe of their yield, furnished on a par with the wealthiest of those treasuries; and the people used to divide the yearly income from the mines among themselves. So when they were founding the treasury, they consulted the Oracle as to whether their present prosperity would last them a long time, and the Pythian prophetess gave them this reply:

At the height of their wealth from gold and silver mines, who refused the exiled Samians a loan and lost a hundred talents and their fields for it — as their oracle about the white council-house had warned them.

## modern-en · aeginetans · 393:0

Amasis became a friend of the Greeks. Among other tokens of friendship, he granted the city of Naucratis to Greeks who came to Egypt, giving them a place to live. For those who did not wish to settle but came on trading voyages, he set aside areas where they could erect altars and sacred precincts to their gods. The largest, most famous, and most used of these is called the Hellenion. It was founded jointly by the following cities: of the Ionians, Chios, Teos, Phocaea, and Clazomenae; of the Dorians, Rhodes, Cnidos, Halicarnassos, and Phaselis; of the Aeolians, Mytilene alone. The Hellenion belongs to these cities, and they are the ones who appoint the market supervisors. Other cities that claim a share have no right to one. Separately, the Aeginetans established a precinct of Zeus, the Samians one of Hera, and the Milesians one of Apollo.

Who with the Cretans defeated the Samian settlers at Kydonia and dedicated the ships’ boar-prows in the temple of Athena on Aegina.

## modern-en · otanes · 465:0

This proclamation, I say, he made as soon as he established himself on the throne. But in the eighth month his identity was discovered, and it came about in this way. There was a certain Otanes son of Pharnaspes, inferior to no Persian in birth or wealth. This Otanes was the first to suspect that the Magian was not Smerdis son of Cyrus but the person he really was, drawing his inference from these facts: that he never went out of the fortress, and that he did not summon any of the distinguished men among the Persians into his presence. Having formed this suspicion, he proceeded as follows. Cambyses had married Otanes' daughter, whose name was Phaidyme; and this same daughter the Magian was now keeping as his wife, living with her as with all the other wives of Cambyses. So Otanes sent a message to this daughter, asking who the man was beside whom she slept—whether Smerdis son of Cyrus or some other. She sent back word that she did not know, for she had never seen Smerdis son of Cyrus, nor did she know otherwise who the man was who lived with her. Otanes then sent a second time and said: “If you yourself do not know Smerdis son of Cyrus, then ask Atossa who this man is with whom both she and you live as wives. For she must surely know her own brother.”

Son of Pharnaspes, the first to suspect that the man on the throne was not Smerdis, and the one who proved it through his own daughter. He argued for democracy against the other six, withdrew from the contest for the throne on condition that his house be free, and it still was in Herodotus’s day.

Then Otanes took with him Aspathines and Gobryas, who were leading men among the Persians and his own most trusted friends, and told them the whole matter. ## modern-en · oibares · 482:0

Now Darius had a clever groom whose name was Oibares. To this man, after they had left their assembly, Darius said: “Oibares, we have resolved about the kingship as follows: that the man whose horse neighs first at sunrise, when we are mounted, shall be king. So if you have any cleverness, contrive that we may win this prize, and no one else.” Oibares replied: “My master, if it truly depends on this whether you be king or not, take heart on this score and keep your courage high, for no other shall be king before you—such are the charms I have at my command.” Then Darius said: “If you have any such trick, now is the time to devise it and not to put it off, for our contest is tomorrow.” Oibares, hearing this, did as follows. As night was falling, he took one of the mares—the one which Darius' horse most preferred—and led her into the suburb of the city and tied her up. Then he brought up Darius' horse, led him around her for some time—bringing him so close that he touched the mare—and finally let the horse mount her.

Darius’s groom, who won him the kingdom before sunrise with a mare, a hand and a horse that neighed first.

## modern-en · parmys · 485:0

So Darius son of Hystaspes had been declared king, and throughout Asia all but the Arabians were his subjects, having been subdued first by Cyrus and then again by Cambyses. The Arabians, however, never submitted to the Persians as subjects, but had become guest-friends when they let Cambyses pass through to Egypt—for without the Arabians' consent, the Persians could not have invaded Egypt. Darius made the most noble marriages possible in the estimation of the Persians. He married two daughters of Cyrus: Atossa and Artystone. Atossa had previously been the wife of Cambyses her brother, and then of the Magian; Artystone was a virgin. Besides them he married the daughter of Smerdis son of Cyrus, whose name was Parmys; and he also took to wife the daughter of Otanes, the man who had exposed the Magian. Everything became filled with his power. And first he had a carving in stone made and set up, showing a man on horseback, and he wrote on it an inscription to this effect: “Darius son of Hystaspes, by the excellence of his horse,”—naming it—“and of his groom Oibares, obtained the kingdom of the Persians.”

Smerdis’s daughter, one of the wives Darius took to fasten the succession to Cyrus’s line.

## modern-en · zopyros · 550:0

Then in the twentieth month a prodigy befell Zopyros, son of that Megabyzos who had been one of the seven men who killed the Magian. To this Zopyros, son of Megabyzos, a prodigy occurred: one of the mules that served as bearers of provisions for him gave birth. When this was reported to him, and Zopyros had himself seen the foal—for he did not believe the report—he charged those who had seen it to tell no one what had happened, and he considered with himself what to do. Bearing in mind the words of the Babylonian who had said at the start that when mules bore young the wall would be taken—remembering, I say, this ominous saying—it seemed to Zopyros that Babylon could be taken. For he thought that both the man had spoken and his mule had foaled by divine dispensation.

Megabyzos’s son, to whom a mule foaled; he cut off his own nose and ears, had himself whipped, deserted to Babylon as a mutilated man with a grievance, was given the city’s army, and handed the walls to Darius. Darius said he would rather have one Zopyros unmutilated than twenty Babylons.

## modern-en · demokedes · 522:0

Polycrates, however, disregarded every counsel and set sail for Oroetes, taking with him, besides many other friends, Demokedes son of Calliphon, a man of Croton who was a physician and practised his art better than anyone else of his time. When he arrived at Magnesia, Polycrates was miserably put to death in a manner unworthy both of himself and of his lofty ambitions. For apart from those who became despots of the Syracusans, none of the other Hellenic despots is worthy to be compared with Polycrates in magnificence. And when Oroetes had killed him in a way not fit to be told, he impaled his body. Of those who had come with him, he released all the Samians, bidding them be grateful to him for being free men; but all those in his company who were either allies or servants, he kept as slaves. Polycrates, then, being hung up, fulfilled his daughter's vision entirely: for he was bathed by Zeus whenever it rained, and anointed by the Sun as he gave off moisture from his body.

The physician of Croton, sold into Persia as Polycrates’s slave, who cured Darius’s ankle and Atossa’s breast, got everything he asked for except his freedom, and talked his way home by way of a reconnaissance of Greece. The two editions spell him Demokedes and Democedes.

## modern-en · milon · 534:0

The Persians, setting sail from there and pursuing Demokedes, reached Croton, and finding him in the market-place, laid hands on him. Some of the men of Croton, fearing Persian power, were willing to let him go; but others took hold of him and struck at the Persians with their staves, while the Persians pleaded: “Men of Croton, take care what you are doing. You are rescuing a man who was a slave of King Darius and ran away from him. How do you think King Darius will be content to receive such an insult? And how can this act be well for you, if you take him away from us? What city, do you think, shall we make an expedition against sooner than this, and what city shall we try to enslave before this?” Saying this, however, they did not persuade the men of Croton. Having had Demokedes rescued from them and the cargo ship they had brought with them seized, they set sail to return to Asia, and did not try to visit or investigate any more parts of Hellas, now that they were deprived of their guide. This, however, Demokedes gave them as a charge when they were putting out to sea: to tell Darius that Demokedes was betrothed to the daughter of Milon. For the wrestler Milon had a great name at the king's court; and I suppose that Demokedes pressed for this marriage, spending a great deal of money to bring it about, so that Darius might see that he was held in honour in his own country as well.

The wrestler of Croton, whose daughter Demokedes bought himself a betrothal to, in name, because Darius had heard of him.

## modern-en · aristophilides · 533:0

So these men, having gone down to Phoenicia and to the city of Sidon there, at once manned two triremes, and besides them loaded a large cargo ship with goods of every kind. Then when they had made everything ready they set sail for Hellas, and touching at various places they viewed the coastal regions and wrote a description, until at last, when they had seen most of the famous places, they arrived at Taras in Italy. There, out of goodwill toward Demokedes, Aristophilides the king of the Tarentines unfastened and removed the steering-oars of the Median ships, and also confined the Persians in prison, alleging they came as spies. While they were being dealt with this way, Demokedes went off and reached Croton. When he was safely in his own native place, Aristophilides set the Persians free and returned to them the parts of their ships he had taken off.

King of the Tarentines, who unshipped the Persian ships’ steering-oars and locked up the crews so that Demokedes could get away to Croton.

## modern-en · gillos · 535:0

The Persians, however, after putting out from Croton, were cast away with their ships in Iapygia. As they were being held there as slaves, Gillos, a Tarentine exile, rescued them and brought them back to King Darius. In return, Darius offered him whatever he desired; and Gillos chose the right to return to Taras, narrating first the story of his misfortune. In order not to disturb all Hellas—as would be the case if on his account a great expedition sailed to invade Italy—he said it was enough for him that the men of Cnidos should be the ones who brought him back, without any others. For he supposed that by their means, since they were friends of the Tarentines, his return from exile could most easily be arranged. Darius accordingly, having promised, carried it out: he sent a message to Cnidos and bade them bring Gillos back to Taras. The men of Cnidos obeyed Darius, but they could not persuade the Tarentines, and were not strong enough to use force. So these things turned out this way. These were the first Persians to come from Asia to Hellas, and for the reason stated, these were sent as spies.

The Tarentine exile who rescued the stranded Persians and brought them back to the king, and asked in payment only to be restored — which the Cnidians could not manage.

## modern-en · indians · 435:0

It is clear to me, therefore, by every kind of proof, that Cambyses was exceedingly mad; for otherwise he would not have undertaken to mock religious rites and customary observances. For if one were to propose to all men a choice, bidding them select the best customs out of all the customs that exist, each race, after examining them all, would choose those of their own people; thus all think their own customs by far the best. And so it is unlikely that anyone but a madman would make jest of such things. That all men are accustomed to think this way about their customs, we may judge by many other proofs and especially by the following. Darius, in the course of his reign, summoned those of the Greeks who were present in his land and asked them for what price they would consent to eat the bodies of their fathers when they died; and they answered that for no price would they do so. After this Darius summoned those Indians who are called Callatians, who eat their parents, and asked them in the presence of the Greeks — who understood what was said by help of an interpreter — for what payment they would consent to burn the bodies of their fathers when they died; and they cried out loud and begged him to keep silence from such words. Thus, then, these things are established by custom, and I think Pindar spoke rightly in his verse when he said that “of all things, law is king.”

The most numerous nation Herodotus knows, whose Callatians eat their dead and who pay their tribute in gold dust.

When the herald had spoken, Cyrus reportedly asked the Greeks in his company who the Spartans were and how many. On hearing the answer, he told the Spartan herald: "I have never yet feared the kind of men who have a special place in the center of their city where they gather to cheat each other with oaths." This was a jab at the Greeks for having marketplaces, something the Persians do not use—they never buy or sell in markets. He added: "If I stay healthy, it will be their own misfortunes they discuss, not those of the Ionians." Cyrus aimed this threat at all the Greeks, since they had marketplaces. He then appointed a Persian named Tabalos as governor of Sardis and gave a Lydian named Pactyas the task of transporting Croesus' gold. Cyrus himself marched back toward Agbatana, taking Croesus with him. He considered the Ionians too unimportant to deal with personally. Babylon, the Bactrians, the Sacae, and the Egyptians—those were his primary concerns. He intended to lead campaigns against them himself and send a subordinate to handle the Ionians.

Darius’s twenty provinces, named in a roll of some forty peoples — Chorasmians, Sogdians, Bactrians, Caspians, Parthians, Sarangians, Paricanians and the rest — each with its assessment in talents. The list is Herodotus’s proof of what the empire actually was: not a conquest story but an accounts book.

## modern-en · targitaos · 562:0

Now the Scythians say their nation is the youngest of all peoples, and that this came about as follows. The first man ever to exist in this region, which was then desert, was one named Targitaos. Of this Targitaos they say—though I for my part do not believe it, but so they say—that his parents were Zeus and a daughter of the river Borysthenes. From some such origin as this, they report, Targitaos sprang, and from him were born three sons, Lipoxaïs, Arpoxaïs, and the youngest, Colaxaïs. In their reign there came down from heaven certain things wrought of gold—a plough, a yoke, a battle-axe, and a cup—and fell on the Scythian land. First the eldest saw them and came near, wanting to take them, but the gold blazed with fire at his approach. When he had gone away, the second approached, and again it did the same. So the gold repelled these two by blazing with fire. But when the third and youngest came up to it, the flame was quenched, and he carried the objects to his own house. The elder brothers, acknowledging the significance of the sign, handed the whole of the kingly power over to the youngest.

The first man in the Scythian account of themselves, born of Zeus and a daughter of the Borysthenes; his three sons divided the kingdom by which of them could pick up the golden plough, yoke, axe and cup without being burnt.

Upon this he drew one of his bows—for up to that time Heracles, they say, used to carry two—and showed her the girdle; then he handed over both the bow and the girdle, which had a golden cup at the end of its clasp. Then, remembering the charge given to her, she did as commanded. One of the three sons Heracles begot on the snake-woman in Hylaia, in the Pontic Greeks’ version of the Scythian origin.

Aristeas, however, son of Caÿstrobios, a man of Proconnesos, said in the verses he composed that he came, possessed by Phoebus, to the land of the Issedonians, and that beyond the Issedonians dwelt the Arimaspians, a one-eyed race, and beyond them the gold-guarding griffins, and beyond them the Hyperboreans extending as far as the sea. All these except the Hyperboreans, beginning with the Arimaspians, were continually making war on their neighbours; and the Issedonians were gradually driven out of their country by the Arimaspians, and the Scythians by the Issedonians, and so the Cimmerians, who dwelt on the southern sea, being pressed by the Scythians, left their land. ## modern-en · anacharsis-scythian · 602:0

Now the region of the Euxine against which Darius was preparing to march contains, apart from the Scythian race, the most ignorant nations of all lands; for we can point to no people in the region of the Pontus distinguished for ability, nor do we know of any learned man who has arisen there, apart from the Scythian nation and Anacharsis. By the Scythians, one thing—the most important of all human matters—has been discovered more cleverly than by any other men we know; in other respects, I have no great admiration for them. That most important thing they have discovered is such that no one who has come to attack them can escape again; and if they do not wish to be found, it is impossible to catch them. For they who have no cities founded, no walls built, but carry their houses with them and are mounted archers, living not from the plough but from cattle, and whose dwellings are upon wagons—these are surely invincible and impossible to approach.

The one Scythian the Greeks admire, killed by his own king for keeping a Greek festival — Herodotus’s single exception, with Skyles, to the rule that Scythians want nothing Greek.

## modern-en · saulios · 632:0

This nation too is very averse to adopting foreign customs, rejecting even those of other tribes among themselves, but especially those of the Hellenes—as the histories of Anacharsis and later of Skyles proved. As for Anacharsis, when he was returning to the abodes of the Scythians after having visited many lands and displayed in them much wisdom, he sailed through the Hellespont and put in to Kyzicos. Finding the people of Kyzicos celebrating a festival with great magnificence in honour of the Mother of the gods, Anacharsis vowed to the Mother that if he returned safe and sound to his own land, he would sacrifice to her with the same rites as he saw the men of Kyzicos perform, and also hold a night festival. So when he came to Scythia, he went down into the region called Hylaia (which runs along the racecourse of Achilles and happens to be quite full of all sorts of trees). Into this, I say, Anacharsis went down and proceeded to perform all the ceremonies of the festival in honour of the goddess, with a kettle-drum and with images hung about his person. One of the Scythians perceived him doing this and declared it to King Saulios; the king came himself, and when he saw Anacharsis doing this, shot him with an arrow and killed him. So at the present time, if one asks about Anacharsis, the Scythians say they do not know him—for this reason, that he had gone out of his own country to Hellas and adopted foreign customs. As I heard from Tymnes the steward of Ariapeithes, he was the paternal uncle of Idanthyrsos king of the Scythians, and the son of Gnuros son of Lycos son of Spargapeithes. If then Anacharsis was of this house, let him know he died by the hand of his brother, for Idanthyrsos was the son of Saulios, and it was Saulios who killed Anacharsis.

King of the Scythians, who shot his brother Anacharsis with an arrow for celebrating the rites of the Mother of the Gods.

## modern-en · octamasades · 636:0

After this, when Skyles was riding out again to his own abode, the Scythians took his brother Octamasades for their leader—a son of the daughter of Teres—and rose in revolt against Skyles. When he perceived what was being done against him and for what reason, he fled for refuge to Thrace. Octamasades, informed of this, marched upon Thrace. When he had come to the river Ister, the Thracians met him; and as they were about to engage in battle, Sitalkes sent a messenger to Octamasades with this word: “Why must we test one another in fight? You are my sister's son, and you hold my brother in your power. Give him back to me, and I will deliver to you your brother Skyles; and let neither of us put our armies in peril, neither you nor I.” Thus Sitalkes proposed through a herald; for a brother of Sitalkes was with Octamasades, having gone into exile for fear of him. Octamasades agreed; by giving up his own maternal uncle to Sitalkes, he received his brother Skyles in exchange. Sitalkes, when he received his brother, led him away as a prisoner, but Octamasades cut off Skyles' head there on the spot. So carefully do the Scythians guard their own customs, and such are the penalties they inflict on those who take foreign customs besides their own.

## modern-en · salmoxis · 650:0

Their belief in immortality is of this kind: they hold that they do not die, but that he who is killed goes to Salmoxis, a divinity (whom some of them call Gebeleizis). At intervals of four years they send one of their own people, chosen by lot, as a messenger to Salmoxis, charging him with such requests as they have to make on each occasion. They send him thus: certain men appointed for this hold three javelins, and others meanwhile take hold of the man being sent to Salmoxis, both by his hands and feet, and first they swing him up, then throw him into the air so that he falls upon the spear points. If he is pierced through and killed, they think the god is favourable to them; but if he is not killed, they find fault with the messenger himself, calling him a worthless man, and then, having faulted him, they send another. They give him the charge beforehand, while he is still alive. These same Thracians also shoot arrows up towards the sky when thunder and lightning come, and use threats against the god, believing that no other god exists except their own.

The divinity of the Getai, whom some of them call Gebeleizis, and whom the Greeks say was a man — a freed slave of Pythagoras who built an underground chamber, disappeared into it for three years, and came back to prove immortality.

## modern-en · pythagoras-samos · 651:0

This Salmoxis, I hear from the Hellenes who dwell about the Hellespont and the Pontus, was a man, and became a slave in Samos—a slave, in fact, of Pythagoras son of Mnesarchos. After becoming free, he gained great wealth and afterwards returned to his own land. Since the Thracians live hardly and are rather simple-minded, this Salmoxis, being acquainted with the Ionian way of life and with manners more cultivated than the Thracians were used to see—for he had associated with Hellenes, and not least with Pythagoras, who was no mean philosopher among them—prepared a banqueting hall, where he received and feasted the chief men of the tribe, instructing them meanwhile that neither he himself nor his guests nor their descendants in succession after them would die; but that they would come to a place where they would live forever and have all things good. While doing and saying these things, he was meanwhile making for himself a chamber under the ground. When his chamber was finished, he disappeared from among the Thracians and went down into the underground chamber, where he continued to live for three years. They grieved for his loss and mourned for him as dead. Then in the fourth year he appeared to the Thracians, and in this way what Salmoxis said became credible to them.

Son of Mnesarchos, named as the master whose slave Salmoxis is supposed to have been — a story Herodotus reports and does not believe.

Darius, having gazed on the Pontus, sailed back to the bridge, of which Mandrocles a Samian had been chief constructor. Having gazed on the Bosphorus as well, he set up beside it two pillars of white stone with characters cut upon them—on one Assyrian, on the other Hellenic—giving the names of all the nations he was leading with him; and he was leading all over whom he ruled. The whole number of them, without the naval force, was reckoned at seventy myriads including cavalry; and ships had been gathered together to the number of six hundred. These pillars the Byzantians later conveyed to their city, after the events of which I speak, and used them for the altar of Artemis Orthosia, except for one stone which was left standing beside the temple of Dionysos in Byzantion, covered with Assyrian characters. Now the place on the Bosphorus where Darius made his bridge is, as I conclude, midway between Byzantion and the temple at the mouth of the Pontus.

The Samian who built the bridge of boats across the Bosphorus, was richly rewarded, and spent the money on a painting of the crossing dedicated in the temple of Hera.

## modern-en · sataspes · 599:0

Thus this country was first known to be what it is. After this, the Carthaginians make report of it. For as to Sataspes son of Teaspis the Achaemenid, he did not sail round Libya, though he was sent for this very purpose; rather, he was struck with fear by the length of the voyage and the desolation of the land, and so returned back without completing the task his mother had laid upon him. This man had outraged a daughter of Zopyros son of Megabyzos, a virgin. When he was about to be impaled by order of King Xerxes for this offence, Sataspes' mother, who was a sister of Darius, entreated for his life, saying she would herself impose on him a greater penalty than Xerxes would: he should be compelled, she said, to sail around Libya, until in sailing around it he came to the Arabian gulf. Xerxes having agreed to these terms, Sataspes went to Egypt and, obtaining a ship and crew from the Egyptians, sailed to the Pillars of Heracles. Having passed through them and rounded the promontory of Libya called Soloeis, he sailed on southwards. Then, after he had traversed much sea over many months, and ever more voyaging was required, he turned around and sailed back to Egypt. Having come from there into the presence of King Xerxes, he reported that at the furthest point he had reached, he was sailing past a dwarfish people who wore clothing made from the palm tree, and who, whenever his ship came to land, left their towns and fled into the mountains. When his men entered the towns, he said, they did no harm, but only took food from them. The reason, he said, why he had not completed the voyage round Libya was that the ship could sail no further and was stuck fast. Xerxes, however, did not believe he was speaking the truth, and since he had not performed the appointed task, impaled him, exacting the penalty pronounced before. A eunuch belonging to Sataspes ran off to Samos as soon as he heard his master was dead, carrying large sums of money. A man of Samos took possession of these—whose name I know, but I deliberately pass over without mention.

The Achaemenid sent to sail round Libya instead of being impaled, who turned back in fear and was impaled after all; his eunuch ran off to Samos with a great sum.
