Darius then, marching through Thrace, arrived at Sestos in the Chersonese, and from there crossed over himself in his ships to Asia; but to command his army in Europe he left Megabazos a Persian—whom Darius once honoured by uttering this saying in the land of Persia. Darius was beginning to eat pomegranates, and at once, when he opened the first, his brother Artabanos asked him of what he would most wish to have as many as there were seeds in the pomegranate. Darius answered that he would wish to have men like Megabazos as many as that in number, rather than to have Hellas subject to him. In Persia, I say, he honoured him by uttering these words; and now he left him in command with eight myriads of his army.

The Persian Darius left to command in Europe — the man whose praise Darius rated above a pomegranate’s seeds; he subdued the Hellespont and told the Persians the Chalcedonians must have been blind.

## modern-en · histiaeus · 693:0

Upon this the Ionians took counsel together. Miltiades the Athenian, who was commander and despot of the men of the Chersonese on the Hellespont, was of the opinion that they should follow the Scythians' advice and set Ionia free. But Histiaios the Milesian was of the opposite opinion. For he said that at present it was by means of Darius that each of them was ruling as despot over a city; and if Darius' power were destroyed, neither could he himself continue to rule the Milesians, nor could any other of them rule any city—for each city would choose popular rather than despotic rule. When Histiaios declared his opinion thus, all at once turned to this opinion, whereas at first they had been adopting Miltiades'.

Tyrant of Miletus, who talked the Ionians out of breaking Darius’s bridge over the Ister on the argument that their own tyrannies depended on him. The two editions spell him Histiaeus and Histiaios.

## modern-en · amazons · 666:0

About the Sauromatai this tale is told. When the Hellenes had fought with the Amazons—now the Amazons are called by the Scythians Oiorpata, a name which in the Hellenic tongue means “slayers of men,” for they call “man” oior, and pata means “to slay”—then, the story goes, the Hellenes, having defeated them in the battle at the Thermodon, were sailing away, carrying with them in three ships as many Amazons as they had been able to take prisoner. These, out on the open sea, set upon the men and threw them out of the ships; but they knew nothing of ships, nor how to use rudders, sails, or oars, and after casting out the men they were driven about by wave and wind and came to that part of the Maeotian lake where Cremnoi stands. Cremnoi is in the land of the free Scythians. There the Amazons disembarked from their ships and made their way into the country; and having first met with a troop of horses feeding, they seized them, and mounted upon these they plundered the property of the Scythians.

Whom the Scythians call Oiorpata, man-slayers; the ones taken at the Thermodon killed their crews, drifted to the Maeotian lake, and became the Sauromatai by marrying Scythian youths on terms.

## modern-en · theras · 703:0

At that very same time Theras, son of Autesion, son of Tisamenus, son of Thersander, son of Polyneices, was preparing to leave Lacedaemon to found a settlement. This Theras was of the line of Cadmus, and was maternal uncle to the sons of Aristodemus, Eurysthenes and Procles. While these nephews were still children, Theras as their guardian held royal power in Sparta. But once his nephews had grown up and taken power into their own hands, Theras—resenting being ruled by others after he had tasted rule himself—declared that he would not remain in Lacedaemon but would sail away to his kinsmen. On the island now called Thera, formerly called Callista, there were descendants of Membliarus, son of Poikiles, a Phoenician. For Cadmus, son of Agenor, while searching for Europa, had put in at the island now called Thera; and whether because the country pleased him once he landed, or for some other reason, he left on this island, along with other Phoenicians, Membliarus, who was one of his own kinsmen. These men had occupied the island called Callista for eight generations before Theras came from Lacedaemon.

The Spartan regent who would not be a subject when his nephews came of age, and led the colony to Callista, which took his name — Thera.

## modern-en · minyae · 145:0

For this reason, then, the Ionians also made twelve cities for themselves; for to say that these are in any way more Ionian than the other Ionians, or have a nobler descent, is mere folly. A large part of them are Abantians from Euboea, who have no share even in the name of Ionia; Minyai of Orchomenos have been mingled with them; also Cadmeians, Dryopians, Phokians who seceded from their native state, Molossians, Pelasgians of Arcadia, Dorians of Epidauros, and many other races have been mingled with them. And those of them who set forth to their settlements from the City Hall of Athens, and who consider themselves the most nobly born of the Ionians — these, I say, brought no women with them to their settlement, but took Carian women, whose parents they slew. On account of this slaughter, these women laid down a rule for themselves, imposing oaths on one another and handing it down to their daughters, that they should never eat with their husbands, nor should a wife call her own husband by name. This was because the Ionians had slain their fathers and husbands and children, and then, having done this, had taken them as wives. This happened at Miletos.

The children of the Argonauts, driven from Lemnos, who camped on Taÿgetus, were taken in by Sparta, plotted, and were saved by their Spartan wives smuggling them out in their own clothes.

## modern-en · etearchus-oaxos · 710:0

This is the account of the Theraeans; and for what follows the Theraeans are in agreement with the men of Cyrene—from this point onward, I say, since concerning Battus the Cyrenaeans tell a completely different story from the Theraeans. Theirs is this: In Crete there is a city called Oaxus, where a man named Etearchus became king. Having a daughter whose mother was dead, named Phronime, he nevertheless took another wife. This woman, coming into the household, decided to be a stepmother to Phronime in deed as well as in name, mistreating her and devising every possible injury against her. In the end she brought a charge of lewdness against her and convinced her husband that it was true. Persuaded by his wife, he devised an unholy plan against his daughter. There was in Oaxus a certain Themison, a merchant of Thera, whom Etearchus took in as a guest-friend and made swear that he would do whatever he was asked. Once he had sworn, Etearchus brought his daughter and handed her over, telling him to take her away and throw her into the sea. Themison was furious at the deceit practiced upon him in the matter of the oath, and dissolved his guest-friendship with Etearchus. He did as follows: he took the girl and sailed away, and when he had reached the open sea, to free himself from the oath he had sworn to Etearchus he tied ropes around her on each side, lowered her into the sea, and then drew her up again—and so came to Thera.

King of Oaxus in Crete, who let his second wife persuade him to swear away his own daughter Phronime — and handed her to a merchant to be drowned. A different man from the Etearchus of the Ammonians in Book 2.

## modern-en · corobius · 707:0

After this there was no rain in Thera for seven years, and in those years all the trees on the island withered up except one. When the Theraeans consulted the oracle, the Pythian priestess gave as the cause this matter of colonizing Libya. Having no remedy for their troubles, they sent messengers to Crete to find out whether any Cretan or any foreigner staying in Crete had ever been to Libya. These men, wandering about the country, came among other places to the city of Itanus, and there they met a murex-fisher named Corobius, who said he had been carried off course by winds and had reached Libya, and in Libya the island of Platea. They persuaded him with a payment of money and took him to Thera. From Thera, at first only a few men set sail to explore; and Corobius guided them to this same island of Platea. They left Corobius there with provisions for a certain number of months, and sailed back themselves as quickly as they could to report about the island to the people of Thera.

The murex-fisher of Crete who had once been blown to Platea and could pilot the Theraeans there; they left him on the island with rations and forgot him for longer than the rations lasted.

The third king of Cyrene, in whose reign the oracle invited all Greeks to come and share out Libyan land.

## modern-en · battus-iii · 717:0

Then Battus, son of Arcesilaus, succeeded to the kingdom. He was lame and unsound in his feet. The Cyrenaeans, in view of the misfortune that had befallen them, sent men to Delphi to ask what form of government they should adopt to live as well as possible; and the Pythian priestess told them to fetch a reformer of their constitution from Mantineia of the Arcadians. The Cyrenaeans made the request accordingly, and the Mantineians gave them the most respected man among their citizens, whose name was Demonax. When this Demonax had come to Cyrene and made careful inquiry into everything, he first caused them to form three tribes, distributing them as follows: one division he made of the Theraeans and their dependents, another of the Peloponnesians and Cretans, and a third of all the islanders. Secondly, for King Battus he set aside landed estates and priesthoods, but all the other powers the kings used to hold he assigned as public rights to the people.

Arcesilaus’s son, lame and unsound in his feet, in whose reign Cyrene sent to Delphi for a constitution and got Demonax of Mantineia. Pheretime was his wife.

## modern-en · arcesilaus-ii · 716:0

This Battus had a son named Arcesilaus who, on becoming king, quarreled with his own brothers until in the end they left for another region of Libya and, acting on their own initiative, founded the city that then and now is called Barca; and at the same time as they founded it, they induced the Libyans to revolt from the Cyrenaeans. After this, Arcesilaus led an expedition against those Libyans who had received his brothers and had also revolted from Cyrene. The Libyans, afraid of him, fled toward the eastern tribes of Libyans; and Arcesilaus pursued them as they fled, until in his pursuit he reached Leucon in Libya. There the Libyans resolved to make a stand. They joined battle and defeated the Cyrenaeans so decisively that seven thousand Cyrenaean hoplites fell on that field. After this disaster, Arcesilaus, being sick and having swallowed a potion, was strangled by his brother Haliarchus; and Haliarchus was killed by treachery by Arcesilaus's wife, whose name was Eryxo.

Battus the Fortunate’s son, who quarrelled with his brothers until they founded Barca, lost seven thousand hoplites at Leucon, and was strangled by his own brother Haliarchus while sick.

## modern-en · arcesilaus-iii · 718:0

During this Battus's reign things continued in this way, but in the reign of his son Arcesilaus there was great disturbance about the offices of the state. For Arcesilaus, son of Battus the Lame and of Pheretime, declared that he would not allow things to remain as Demonax of Mantineia had arranged them, and demanded back the royal rights of his forefathers. After this he stirred up strife, was defeated, and went into exile to Samos, while his mother went to Salamis in Cyprus. At that time the ruler of Salamis was Euelthon—the same man who dedicated as an offering at Delphi the censer well worth seeing, which is placed in the treasury of the Corinthians. Pheretime came to him and asked him for an army to restore herself and her son to Cyrene. But Euelthon was ready to give her anything else rather than that. Such was the answer the Pythian priestess gave to Arcesilaus. He, taking with him those in Samos, returned to Cyrene. Of these, some escaped the country altogether, but some Arcesilaus got into his hands and sent off to Cyprus to be put to death. These were driven off course to Cnidus, and the Cnidians rescued them and sent them away to Thera. He had as wife a kinswoman of his own, the daughter of the king of Barca whose name was Alazeir. He went to him; and certain Barcans, together with some of the Cyrenaean exiles, noticing him walking in the marketplace, killed him, and killed his father-in-law Alazeir along with him. So Arcesilaus, whether willingly or unwillingly, by misreading the oracle fulfilled his own fate.

But much more about them is reported by the people of Delos than by any others. They say that sacred offerings bound up in wheat straw are carried from the land of the Hyperboreans and come to the Scythians, and from the Scythians the neighbouring nations in succession receive them and convey them westwards, finally as far as the Adriatic. From there they are sent on towards the south; the people of Dodona receive them first of all the Hellenes, and from these they come down to the Malian gulf and are passed over to Euboea, where city sends them on to city till they reach Carystos. But at first, they say, the Hyperboreans sent two maidens bearing the sacred offerings, whose names, the Delians say, were Hyperoche and Laodike. With them, for their protection, the Hyperboreans sent five men of their nation to attend them—those who are now called Perphereës and receive great honour on Delos. But since the Hyperboreans found that those sent away did not come back, they were troubled at the thought of always having to send out and never receive back; so they carried the offerings, bound up in wheat straw, to the borders of their land, and laid a charge upon their neighbours, bidding them pass them on to another nation. These, they say, come to Delos by being passed on in this way. And I know of my own knowledge that a thing is done which resembles these offerings: the women of Thrace and Paionia, when they sacrifice to Artemis “the Queen,” never make their offerings without wheat straw.

## modern-en · arge · 591:0

The maidens, I say, receive this honour from the dwellers in Delos. The same people say that Arge and Opis also, being maidens, came to Delos, passing from the Hyperboreans by the same nations mentioned, even before Hyperoche and Laodike. The latter, they say, came bearing for Eileithuia the tribute they had laid upon themselves for a speedy delivery in childbirth; but Arge and Opis came with the divinities themselves, and other honours have been assigned to them by the people of Delos. The women, they say, collect offerings for them, naming them by their names in the hymn which Olen, a man of Lycia, composed in their honour; and both the natives of the other islands and the Ionians have learnt from them to sing hymns naming Opis and Arge and taking up collections. This Olen came from Lycia and composed also the other ancient hymns sung on Delos. Moreover, they say that when the thighs of the victim are consumed on the altar, the ashes are thrown upon the tomb of Opis and Arge. Their tomb is behind the temple of Artemis, turned towards the east, close to the banqueting hall of the Keians.

One of two earlier Hyperborean maidens who came to Delos with the gods themselves.

On his march toward Babylon, Cyrus reached the river Gyndes. This river rises in the mountains of the Matienians, flows through Dardanian territory, and empties into the Tigris, which passes the city of Opis and flows into the Red Sea. As Cyrus attempted to cross the Gyndes, which was deep enough to be navigable, one of his sacred white horses charged into the river and tried to swim across. The current swept the horse under and carried it away. Cyrus was furious at the river for this outrage. He swore he would make it so weak that women could cross it without getting their knees wet. He suspended his march on Babylon, divided his army in two, and had them dig one hundred and eighty channels on each side of the river—three hundred and sixty in all—fanning out in every direction. This vast project took the entire summer.

## modern-en · tauroi · 655:0

Now in front of Scythia, in the direction towards the sea, lies Thrace; and where a bay is formed in this land, Scythia begins, into which the Ister runs out, the mouth of the river facing the south-east wind. Beginning at the Ister, I am about to describe the coast land of Scythia proper with regard to measurement. From the Ister begins the original land of Scythia, which lies towards the midday and the south wind, and extends as far as the city called Carkinitis. After this, the part that still lies on the coast of the same sea, a country which is mountainous and projects towards the Pontus, is occupied by the Tauric race, as far as the peninsula called the “Rugged Chersonese”; and this extends to the sea which lies towards the east wind. For two sides of the Scythian boundaries lie along the sea—one on the south, the other on the east—just as with Attica. The Tauroi, in truth, occupy a part of Scythia much resembling Attica; it is as if in Attica another race, not the Athenians, occupied the hill region of Sunion (supposing it to project more sharply at the point into the sea), the region cut off by a line from Thoricos to Anaphlystos. Such, if we may compare small things like this with great, is the shape of the Tauric land. For one who has not sailed along that part of the coast of Attica, I will make it clear by another comparison: it is as if in Iapygia another race, not the Iapygians, had cut off for themselves and were holding that extremity of the land bounded by a line beginning at the harbour of Brentesion and running to Taras. In mentioning these two similar cases, I am suggesting many other things as well to which the Tauric land has resemblance.

They followed her; and having come to the river, she watered the horse, and having watered him and filled her jar with water, she came back along the same road, carrying the water on her head, leading the horse after her by the bridle round her arm, and at the same time turning the spindle.

## modern-en · aristagoras-miletus · 791:0

So the Parians had reformed the Milesians. But at the time of which I speak, troubles began to come upon Ionia from these very states, in the following way. From Naxos certain men of the wealthier class were driven into exile by the people, and in their exile they came to Miletus. It happened that Miletus was then under the rule of Aristagoras, son of Molpagoras, who was both son-in-law and cousin of Histiaeus, son of Lysagoras, whom Darius was keeping at Susa. For Histiaeus was tyrant of Miletus, and it happened that he was at Susa at this time when the Naxians came, who had in former times been guest-friends of Histiaeus. When the Naxians arrived, they asked Aristagoras whether he would supply them with a force, so that they might return from exile to their own land. And he, thinking that if they returned to their state through his means he would be ruler of Naxos, but at the same time making a pretext of the guest-friendship with Histiaeus, made them this proposal: “I am not able to promise that I can supply you with force sufficient to bring you back from exile against the will of those Naxians who hold power in the state; for I hear that the Naxians have an army eight thousand shields strong and many warships. But I will use every effort to devise a way; and my plan is this. Artaphrenes happens to be my friend. Now Artaphrenes, you should know, is a son of Hystaspes and brother of King Darius; and he is ruler of all the coastal peoples of Asia, with a great army and many ships. He, I think, will do whatever we ask of him.” Hearing this, the Naxians turned the matter over to Aristagoras to manage as best he could, and they bade him promise gifts and the expenses of the expedition, saying that they would pay them; for they had every expectation that, once they appeared at Naxos, the Naxians would do all their bidding, and likewise the other islanders. For none of these islands, that is to say the Cyclades, was as yet subject to Darius.

Son of Molpagoras, deputy tyrant of Miletus, who talked Artaphrenes into the Naxos expedition, lost it, started the Ionian revolt to save himself, was refused by Sparta and promised twenty ships by Athens, and ran away twice — the second time to his death among the Thracians. Herodotus does not admire him.

The Lacedaemonians, since the same utterance was delivered to them on all occasions, sent Anchimolius son of Aster, a man of repute among their citizens, with an army to drive the sons of Peisistratus out of Athens—even though these were very closely connected with them by guest-friendship; for they held that the concerns of the god should be preferred to those of men. This force they sent by sea in ships. Anchimolius, having put in to shore at Phalerum, disembarked his army; but the sons of Peisistratus, having learned of this beforehand, called in an auxiliary force from Thessaly, for they had made an alliance with the Thessalians, and the Thessalians at their request sent by public resolution a body of a thousand horse and also their king Cineas, a man of Conium. With these as allies, the sons of Peisistratus devised the following: they cut down the trees in the plain of Phalerum and made this district fit for horsemen to ride over, and then they sent the cavalry to attack the enemy's camp; and falling upon it, they killed (among many other Lacedaemonians) Anchimolius himself, and the survivors they shut up in their ships. Such was the outcome of the first expedition from Lacedaemon; and the burial-place of Anchimolius is at Alopece in Attica, near the temple of Heracles at Cynosarges.

I have now told of the vision Hipparchus saw in his dream, and also the descent of the Gephyraeans, to whom the murderers of Hipparchus belonged; and in addition to this I must take up and continue the story I was about to tell at first—how the Athenians were freed from their tyrants. While Hippias was tyrant and was dealing harshly with the Athenians because of the death of Hipparchus, the Alcmaeonidae, who were of Athenian race and were fugitives from the sons of Peisistratus, failed in an attempt made together with the other Athenian exiles to return by force; and when they tried to return and set Athens free, they met with a great disaster, after having fortified Leipsydrium, which lies above Paeonia. These Alcmaeonidae, still devising every means against the sons of Peisistratus, accepted the contract to build and complete the temple at Delphi—that which now exists but did not as yet at that time. Being already both wealthy and of old repute, they completed the temple in a manner more splendid than the contract required, particularly in this: that having agreed to make the temple of common limestone, they built the front portions of it in Parian marble.

The Athenian family in exile who, Herodotus says, bribed the Pythian priestess to tell every Spartan who came that Athens must be set free — and so brought down the tyranny.

## modern-en · cleisthenes-athens · 827:0

Athens, which even before that time was great, then, once it had been freed from tyrants, became gradually greater still; and in it two men exercised power—Cleisthenes, a descendant of Alcmaeon, the same man who is reported to have bribed the Pythian priestess, and Isagoras, son of Tisander, of a family highly reputed, though of his original descent I am unable to say; his kinsmen, however, sacrifice to the Carian Zeus. These men came into party strife over power; and when Cleisthenes was being worsted in the struggle, he made common cause with the people. After this he caused the Athenians to be divided into ten tribes, who were formerly in four; and he changed the names that they had been known by after the sons of Ion—Geleon, Aegicoreus, Argades, and Hoples—and invented for them names taken from other heroes, all native Athenians except Ajax, whom he added as a neighbor and ally, though he was no Athenian.

The Alcmaeonid who beat Isagoras by taking the people into his party, made ten tribes out of four, and was expelled by Cleomenes as one of the accursed — and sent for again.

## modern-en · cleisthenes-sicyon · 828:0

In these matters it seems to me that this Cleisthenes was imitating his mother's father, Cleisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon. For when that Cleisthenes went to war with Argos, he first put a stop in Sicyon to the contests of rhapsodes, which were concerned with the poems of Homer, because Argives and Argos are praised in them almost everywhere. Secondly, since there was (as there still is) in the very marketplace of the Sicyonians a hero-shrine of Adrastus, son of Talaus, Cleisthenes conceived a desire to cast him out of the land because he was an Argive. So he came to Delphi and consulted the oracle as to whether he should cast Adrastus out; and the Pythian priestess answered that Adrastus was king of the Sicyonians, whereas he was a stoner of them. Since the god did not permit him to do this, he went away home and considered means by which Adrastus might be brought to leave of his own accord; and when he thought he had discovered them, he sent to Thebes in Boeotia and said that he wished to introduce Melanippus, son of Astacus, into his city, and the Thebans gave him leave. So Cleisthenes introduced Melanippus into his city, appointed a sacred enclosure for him within the precincts of the city hall itself, and established him there in the strongest position. Cleisthenes introduced Melanippus (for I must report this too) because he was the greatest enemy of Adrastus, having killed both his brother Mecisteus and his son-in-law Tydeus. Once he had appointed the sacred enclosure for him, Cleisthenes took away the sacrifices and festivals of Adrastus and gave them to Melanippus. Now the Sicyonians had been accustomed to honor Adrastus with very great honors; for this land was formerly the land of Polybus, and Adrastus was the son of Polybus's daughter, and Polybus, dying without sons, gave his kingdom to Adrastus. The Sicyonians accordingly gave other honors to Adrastus, but especially, with reference to his sufferings, they honored him with tragic choruses, paying this honor not to Dionysus but to Adrastus. Cleisthenes, however, gave the choruses back to Dionysus, and the other rites besides these he gave to Melanippus.

Tyrant of Sicyon and the Athenian Cleisthenes’s mother’s father, who renamed the Dorian tribes after a pig, an ass and a swine and called his own the Rulers, and tried to turn Adrastus out of his own hero-shrine by importing Melanippus.

For when that Cleisthenes went to war with Argos, he first put a stop in Sicyon to the contests of rhapsodes, which were concerned with the poems of Homer, because Argives and Argos are praised in them almost everywhere. Secondly, since there was (as there still is) in the very marketplace of the Sicyonians a hero-shrine of Adrastus, son of Talaus, Cleisthenes conceived a desire to cast him out of the land because he was an Argive. So he came to Delphi and consulted the oracle as to whether he should cast Adrastus out; and the Pythian priestess answered that Adrastus was king of the Sicyonians, whereas he was a stoner of them. Since the god did not permit him to do this, he went away home and considered means by which Adrastus might be brought to leave of his own accord; and when he thought he had discovered them, he sent to Thebes in Boeotia and said that he wished to introduce Melanippus, son of Astacus, into his city, and the Thebans gave him leave. So Cleisthenes introduced Melanippus into his city, appointed a sacred enclosure for him within the precincts of the city hall itself, and established him there in the strongest position. Cleisthenes introduced Melanippus (for I must report this too) because he was the greatest enemy of Adrastus, having killed both his brother Mecisteus and his son-in-law Tydeus. Once he had appointed the sacred enclosure for him, Cleisthenes took away the sacrifices and festivals of Adrastus and gave them to Melanippus. Now the Sicyonians had been accustomed to honor Adrastus with very great honors; for this land was formerly the land of Polybus, and Adrastus was the son of Polybus's daughter, and Polybus, dying without sons, gave his kingdom to Adrastus. The Sicyonians accordingly gave other honors to Adrastus, but especially, with reference to his sufferings, they honored him with tragic choruses, paying this honor not to Dionysus but to Adrastus. Cleisthenes, however, gave the choruses back to Dionysus, and the other rites besides these he gave to Melanippus.

Adrastus’s father. The older translation spells him Talaos.

So they spoke; but the majority of the allies did not approve of their words. The rest kept silent, but the Corinthian Socles spoke as follows: “Surely now the heavens shall be beneath the earth, and the earth raised up high above the heavens; men shall have their dwelling in the sea, and fishes that habitation which men had before—seeing that you, Lacedaemonians, are doing away with free governments and are preparing to bring tyranny back into our cities, than which there is nothing more unjust or more murderous among men. For if this really seems good to you—that cities should be ruled by tyrants—then you yourselves first set up a tyrant in your own state, and then try to establish them for others. Yet had you had experience of it, as we have had, you would be able to contribute juster opinions about it than you do now. For the established order of the Corinthian state was this: the government was an oligarchy, and the oligarchs, who were called the Bacchiadae, controlled the state and intermarried among themselves. One of these men, named Amphion, had a daughter born to him who was lame, and her name was Labda. Since none of the Bacchiadae was willing to marry her, she was taken to wife by Aëtion son of Echecrates, of the deme of Petra, but by descent a Lapith and of the race of Caeneus. ## modern-en · onesilus · 865:0

The Cypriots too, except for those of Amathus, were added voluntarily to their alliance; for these also had revolted from the Medes in the following way. There was a certain Onesilus, younger brother of Gorgus king of Salamis, and son of Chersis, the son of Siromus, the son of Euelthon. This man, too, had often in the past advised Gorgus to revolt from the king, and now, when he heard that the Ionians had revolted, he pressed him hard and tried to urge him to it. When he could not persuade Gorgus, Onesilus watched for a time when Gorgus had gone out of the city of Salamis, and then together with the men of his own faction he shut him out of the gates. Gorgus, robbed of the city, took refuge with the Medes, and Onesilus became ruler of Salamis and tried to persuade all the men of Cyprus to join him in revolt. Most he persuaded; but since those of Amathus were not willing to do as he wished, he sat down before their city and besieged it.

Gorgus’s younger brother, who shut him out of Salamis and led the Cyprian revolt; his head was hung over the gate of Amathus and a swarm of bees filled it, which made him a hero with an annual sacrifice.

Meanwhile, while the news about Sardis was going up to the king, and while Darius, after doing what he did with the bow, was coming to speech with Histiaeus, and Histiaeus, having been let go by Darius, was making his way to the coast—during all this time the following events were taking place. As Onesilus of Salamis was besieging those of Amathus, it was reported to him that Artybius, a Persian, bringing with him on ships a large Persian army, was expected soon to arrive in Cyprus. On receiving this news, Onesilus sent heralds to various places in Ionia to summon the Ionians to his aid; and they took counsel together and came without delay with a large force. The Ionians arrived in Cyprus just at the time when the Persians, having crossed over from Cilicia in ships, were proceeding by land to attack Salamis, while the Phoenicians with the ships were sailing around the headland called the “Keys of Cyprus.”

The Persian commander in Cyprus whose horse was trained to rear against a man, and which Onesilus’s Carian groom cut the legs from.

## modern-en · pixodarus · 878:0

Daurises directed his march to the cities on the Hellespont and took Dardanus and Abydos and Percote and Lampsacus and Paesus—taking one of these on each day. But as he was marching from Paesus against the city of Parium, the report came that the Carians had made common cause with the Ionians and were in revolt from the Persians. He therefore turned back from the Hellespont and marched his army upon Caria. As it happened, a report of this was brought to the Carians before Daurises arrived; and on being informed, the Carians gathered at the place called the “White Pillars,” and at the river Marsyas, which flows from the region of Idrias and empties into the Maeander. When the Carians had gathered there, among many counsels offered, the best, in my opinion, was that of Pixodarus son of Mausolus, a man of Cindye, who was married to the daughter of Syennesis king of the Cilicians. His opinion was that the Carians should cross the Maeander and engage the Persians with the river at their backs, so that the Carians, being unable to flee backwards and compelled to remain where they were, might prove themselves even braver in the fight than they naturally would. This opinion did not prevail; they resolved instead that the Persians rather than themselves should have the Maeander at their backs—clearly so that if the Persians were put to flight and worsted, they might never return home but fall into the river.

The Carian who advised crossing the Maeander and fighting with the river at their backs so that the Carians could not run — advice they did not take.

The leader of this ambush was Heraclides son of Ibanollis, a man of Mylasa.

## modern-en · paeonians · 605:0

These are the native Scythian rivers that join to swell its stream, while from the Agathyrsians flows the Maris, which joins the Ister. From the summits of Haimos flow three other great rivers towards the north wind and fall into it: Atlas, Auras, and Tibisis. Through Thrace and the Thracian Crobyzians flow the rivers Athrys, Noes, and Artanes, running into the Ister; and from the Paionians and Mount Rhodope the river Kios, cutting through Haimos in the middle, also runs into it. From the Illyrians the river Angros flows northwards and runs out into the Triballian plain and into the river Brongos, and the Brongos flows into the Ister; thus the Ister receives both these great rivers. From the region above the Ombricans, the river Carpis and another river, the Alpis, also flow towards the north wind and run into it; for the Ister in fact flows through the whole of Europe, beginning in the land of the Celts, who after the Kynesians dwell furthest west of all the peoples of Europe. Flowing thus through all Europe, it falls into the sea alongside Scythia.

Whose two brothers’ scheme brought Darius’s order to move the whole nation to Asia; those round Lake Prasias, living on platforms over the water, were never taken.

## modern-en · perinthians · 762:0

Meanwhile those of the Persians who had been left behind in Europe by Darius, under the command of Megabazus, had subdued first the people of Perinthus among the Hellespontians, since they refused to be subjects of Darius. These had in earlier days also been roughly handled by the Paeonians; for the Paeonians from the Strymon had been ordered by an oracle of their god to march against the Perinthians—and if, when encamped opposite them, the Perinthians should shout aloud and call to them by name, they were to attack; but if they did not shout to them, they were not to attack. This is what the Paeonians set out to do. When the Perinthians were encamped opposite them in the suburb of their city, a challenge was made and a single combat took place in three forms: man against man, horse against horse, and dog against dog. On the tenth day after he received the surrender of the fortress of Memphis, Cambyses set the king of the Egyptians Psammenitos, who had been king for six months, to sit in the suburb of the city, in order to humiliate him. Him, along with other Egyptians, he placed there, and proceeded to test his spirit as follows. Having dressed his daughter in the clothing of a slave, he sent her out with a pitcher to fetch water, and with her he sent other maidens also, chosen from the daughters of the leading men, dressed just as the king's daughter was. As the maidens passed by their fathers with cries and lamentation, the rest of the men began to cry out and lament aloud, seeing their children being ill-used. But Psammenitos, when he saw it before his eyes and perceived what was happening, bent himself down to the earth. Then, after the water-bearers had passed by, Cambyses next sent his son together with two thousand other Egyptians of the same age, with ropes around their necks and bits placed in their mouths; and these were being led away to execution to avenge the death of the Mytilenians who had been destroyed at Memphis with their ship — for the Royal Judges had decided that for each man, ten of the noblest Egyptians should lose their lives in retaliation. When Psammenitos saw them passing by him and perceived that his son was leading the way to death, he did the same as he had done for his daughter, while the other Egyptians sitting around him lamented and showed signs of grief. When these too had passed by, it happened that a man of his table companions, advanced in years, who had been stripped of all his possessions and had nothing beyond what a beggar owns, and was asking alms from the soldiers, passed by Psammenitos son of Amasis and the Egyptians sitting in the suburb of the city. When Psammenitos saw him, he uttered a great cry of lamentation, called his companion by name, and beat himself on the head. Now there were, it seems, men set to watch him, who reported to Cambyses everything he did on each occasion as they passed. Cambyses marveled at what he had done and sent a messenger to ask him: “Psammenitos, your master Cambyses asks you why, when you saw your daughter mistreated and your son going to his death, you did not cry out or lament for them, whereas you honored with these signs of grief the beggar who, as he hears from others, is in no way related to you?” Thus he asked, and the other answered: “O son of Cyrus, my own troubles were too great to lament aloud, but my companion's trouble called for tears, seeing that he has been stripped of great wealth and has come to beggary on the threshold of old age.” When this saying was reported by the messenger, it seemed to them well spoken. And, as the Egyptians report, Croesus shed tears — for he too, as fortune would have it, had accompanied Cambyses to Egypt — and the Persians present shed tears also, and some pity entered into Cambyses himself. He ordered that the life of Psammenitos's son be spared from among those being put to death, and he also ordered that Psammenitos himself be raised from his place in the suburb of the city and brought into his presence.

Who stoned Coës to death as soon as Aristagoras deposed him.

Perceiving these things, Anaxilaus, tyrant of Rhegium, who was at odds with those of Zancle, communicated with the Samians and persuaded them that they should leave the Fair Strand alone, to which they were sailing, and take possession of Zancle instead, since it was now without men to defend it. The Samians did as he said and took possession of Zancle. The men of Zancle, when they were informed that their city was in enemy hands, set out to rescue it and called on Hippocrates, tyrant of Gela, to help them, for he was their ally. But when Hippocrates too had come up with his army to their rescue, he first put Scythes the ruler of the Zanclaeans in fetters, on the ground that he had been the cause of the city's loss, and together with him his brother Pythogenes, and sent them off to the town of Inyx. He then betrayed the cause of the remaining Zanclaeans by coming to terms with the Samians and exchanging oaths with them; in return for this, it had been promised by the Samians that Hippocrates should receive as his share half of all the movable goods in the city and of the slaves, and the whole of the property in the fields round about. So the greater part of the Zanclaeans he put in bonds and kept as slaves for himself, but the chief men among them, three hundred in number, he handed over to the Samians to put to death—which, however, the Samians did not do.

He then betrayed the cause of the remaining Zanclaeans by coming to terms with the Samians and exchanging oaths with them; in return for this, it had been promised by the Samians that Hippocrates should receive as his share half of all the movable goods in the city and of the slaves, and the whole of the property in the fields round about. So the greater part of the Zanclaeans he put in bonds and kept as slaves for himself, but the chief men among them, three hundred in number, he handed over to the Samians to put to death—which, however, the Samians did not do.

Scythes’s brother, put in fetters with him and sent off to Inyx.

So the Parians had reformed the Milesians. But at the time of which I speak, troubles began to come upon Ionia from these very states, in the following way. It happened that Miletus was then under the rule of Aristagoras, son of Molpagoras, who was both son-in-law and cousin of Histiaeus, son of Lysagoras, whom Darius was keeping at Susa. For Histiaeus was tyrant of Miletus, and it happened that he was at Susa at this time when the Naxians came, who had in former times been guest-friends of Histiaeus. When the Naxians arrived, they asked Aristagoras whether he would supply them with a force, so that they might return from exile to their own land. And he, thinking that if they returned to their state through his means he would be ruler of Naxos, but at the same time making a pretext of the guest-friendship with Histiaeus, made them this proposal: “I am not able to promise that I can supply you with force sufficient to bring you back from exile against the will of those Naxians who hold power in the state; for I hear that the Naxians have an army eight thousand shields strong and many warships. But I will use every effort to devise a way; and my plan is this. Artaphrenes happens to be my friend. Now Artaphrenes, you should know, is a son of Hystaspes and brother of King Darius; and he is ruler of all the coastal peoples of Asia, with a great army and many ships. He, I think, will do whatever we ask of him.” Hearing this, the Naxians turned the matter over to Aristagoras to manage as best he could, and they bade him promise gifts and the expenses of the expedition, saying that they would pay them; for they had every expectation that, once they appeared at Naxos, the Naxians would do all their bidding, and likewise the other islanders. The inhabitants of this Chersonese were Dolonkian Thracians; and these Dolonkians, being hard pressed in war by the Apsinthians, sent their kings to Delphi to consult the oracle about the war. At this time, being informed that the Phoenicians were at Tenedos, he filled five triremes with the property he had at hand and sailed away for Athens. In command of this ship, as it happened, was Metiochus, the eldest of Miltiades's sons—not born of the daughter of Olorus the Thracian, but of another woman. The Phoenicians captured him along with his ship; and being informed that he was the son of Miltiades, they brought him up to the king, thinking they would lay up for themselves a great obligation, because it was Miltiades who had declared his opinion to the Ionians that they should do as the Scythians said, at the time when the Scythians asked them to break up the bridge of boats and sail away to their own land. Darius, however, when the Phoenicians brought Metiochus son of Miltiades up to him, did Metiochus no harm, but on the contrary very much good: he gave him a house and possessions and a Persian wife, by whom he had children born who have been ranked as Persians. ## modern-en · euagoras · 989:0

When the Athenians learned of this, they too marched out to Marathon to defend their territory, led by ten generals. The tenth of these was Miltiades, whose father Cimon son of Stesagoras had been forced to go into exile from Athens on account of Pisistratus son of Hippocrates. While in exile, Cimon happened to win a victory at the Olympic games with the four-horse chariot, matching in this achievement his half-brother Miltiades, who had the same mother. Then at the next Olympics he won again with the same mares but allowed Pisistratus to be proclaimed the victor; by handing over the victory he was permitted to return home under an agreement for peace. After he had won yet again at a later Olympic festival with the same mares, it was his fate to be killed by the sons of Pisistratus — Pisistratus himself being no longer alive. They sent men to ambush him by night near the City Hall and had him killed there. Cimon's grave is in the outer part of the city, across the road called the Hollow Way, and directly opposite him are buried those mares that had won him three Olympic victories. The mares of Euagoras the Laconian achieved the same feat, but no others did. Now at that time the elder of Cimon's sons, Stesagoras, was being raised in the house of his uncle Miltiades in the Chersonese, while the younger was being brought up at Athens with Cimon himself, bearing the name Miltiades after Miltiades the founder of the colony in the Chersonese.

These men had occupied the island called Callista for eight generations before Theras came from Lacedaemon.

## modern-en · argeia · 938:0

For the Lacedaemonians, who on this matter agree with none of the poets, say that Aristodemus son of Aristomachus, son of Cleodaeus, son of Hyllus, being their king, himself led them (and not the sons of Aristodemus) to this land which they now possess. Then, not long afterward, the wife of Aristodemus, whose name was Argeia—she was the daughter, they say, of Autesion son of Tisamenus son of Thersander son of Polyneices—is said to have borne twins; and Aristodemus lived only long enough to see his children, and then ended his life by sickness. The Lacedaemonians of that time resolved, according to established custom, to make the elder of the children their king; but they did not know which of them they should take, because they were alike and of equal size. When they were unable to find out, or even before this, they inquired of their mother; but she said that even she herself did not know one from the other. This she said, although she actually knew quite well, because she desired that somehow both might be made kings. The Lacedaemonians were therefore in a difficulty; and being in a difficulty, they sent to Delphi to ask what they should do in the matter. The Pythian priestess bade them regard both children as their kings, but honor most the first in age. So, they say, did the priestess give them her answer; and when the Lacedaemonians were no less at a loss how to find out the elder of them, a Messenian named Panites made a suggestion to them. This Panites, I say, suggested to the Lacedaemonians that they watch the mother and see which of the children she washed and fed first of the two; and if she was seen to do this always in the same order, they would have all they were seeking and wished to discover; but if she too was uncertain and did it in a different order at different times, it would be plain to them that she had no more knowledge than anyone else, and they must turn to some other way. The Spartans, following the Messenian's suggestion, watched the mother of the sons of Aristodemus and found that she gave preference thus to the firstborn, both in feeding and in washing, not knowing she was being watched. They therefore took the child honored by its mother and brought it up in the public hall as the firstborn, and named it Eurysthenes; and the other was called Procles. When they had grown up, both of them, they say, were at variance with one another throughout their whole lives, although they were brothers, and their descendants continued in the same way.

Aristodemus’s wife, who told the Lacedaemonians she could not tell her twins apart. She knew perfectly well. She wanted both of them made kings.

## modern-en · hyllus · 79:0

So when the armies had met in that plain in front of the city of Sardis—a plain wide and open, through which flow rivers (and especially the river Hyllus), all rushing down to join the largest, called the Hermus, which flows from the mountain sacred to the Mother surnamed “of Dindymus” and runs out into the sea by the city of Phocaea—then Cyrus, when he saw the Lydians being arrayed for battle, fearing their horsemen, did as Harpagus the Mede suggested. He gathered all the camels in the train of his army that were carrying provisions and baggage, took off their burdens, and set men upon them equipped like cavalry. Having thus furnished them, he ordered them to go in front of the rest of the army toward the horsemen of Croesus; and after the camel-troop he commanded the infantry to follow; and behind the infantry he placed his whole force of cavalry. When all his men had been placed in their several positions, he charged them to spare none of the rest of the Lydians, slaying all who came in their way, but they were not to kill Croesus himself, not even if he should resist when he was captured. Such was his charge. He had set the camels opposite the horsemen for this reason: because the horse is afraid of the camel and cannot endure either to see its shape or to scent its smell. For this reason, then, the trick had been devised, in order that the cavalry of Croesus might be useless—the very force with which the Lydian king expected most to shine. And as they were coming together to battle, as soon as the horses scented the camels and saw them, they turned back, and the hopes of Croesus were at once brought to nothing. The Lydians, however, did not behave as cowards on that account, but when they perceived what was happening, they leapt from their horses and fought the Persians on foot. At length, however, when many had fallen on either side, the Lydians turned to flight; and having been driven within the wall of their fortress, they were besieged by the Persians.

Heracles’s son, at the head of the Spartan royal descent.

This is the account given by the Lacedaemonians alone of all the Hellenes; but what follows I write in accordance with the general report of the Hellenes: namely, that the names of these kings of the Dorians are correctly enumerated by the Hellenes back to Perseus son of Danaë (leaving out the god), and are shown to be of Hellenic stock—for from that point they were already reckoned as Hellenes. I said “up to Perseus,” and did not trace the descent from a yet higher point, because no name of a mortal father is given for Perseus, as Amphitryon is for Heracles. With good reason, then, I have said “rightly up to Perseus”; but if one enumerates their ancestors in succession going back from Danaë daughter of Acrisius, the rulers of the Dorians will prove to be Egyptians by direct descent.

## modern-en · helots · 945:0

When many thousands of these and of the Helots and of the Spartans themselves have been gathered together in the same place, with their women intermingled, they beat their foreheads with a will and make lamentation without stint, saying that the one who has died last of their kings was the best of all. Whenever any of their kings has been killed in war, they prepare an image to represent him, laid on a couch with fine coverings, and carry it out to be buried. After the burial, no assembly is held among them for ten days, nor any meeting for the choice of magistrates; but they keep mourning during these days. In another respect too they resemble the Persians: when the king is dead and another is appointed king, this newly incoming king releases any Spartan who was a debtor to the king or to the state—just as among the Persians the new king who comes to the throne remits to all the cities the arrears of tribute due.

The Lacedaemonian serfs: gathered in thousands to mourn a dead king, set to pile brushwood round the grove at Argos, sent to drag the priest of Hera from his own altar. One of them was frightened into handing Cleomenes a knife.

Some say in addition that the Pythian prophetess also set forth to him the order of things that is now established for the Spartans; but the Lacedaemonians themselves say that Lycurgus, having become guardian of Leobotes, his brother’s son, who was king of the Spartans, brought in these things from Crete. For as soon as he became guardian he changed all the prevailing laws and took measures that they should not transgress his institutions. After this Lycurgus established what pertains to war—namely the Enomoties and the Triecades and the Common Meals—and, in addition, the Ephors and the Senate. Having made these changes, the Spartans had good laws; and to Lycurgus, after he was dead, they erected a temple, and they pay him great honor. These are their privileges in war; and in peacetime things have been assigned to them as follows. If any sacrifice is performed at public expense, it is the kings' privilege to sit down to the feast before all others, and for the attendants to begin with them first, and to serve each of them a portion double that given to the other guests; they shall have the first pouring of libations and the hides of the animals slain in sacrifice. On every new moon and seventh day of the month, each of them shall be delivered at public expense a full-grown victim at the temple of Apollo, a measure of barley-groats, and a Laconian quarter of wine; at all the games they shall have seats of honor specially set aside for them. Moreover, it is their privilege to appoint as protectors of strangers (proxenoi) whomever they wish of the citizens, and each to choose two “Pythians” (now the Pythians are men sent to consult the god at Delphi, and they eat with the kings at public expense). If the kings do not come to the public dinner, the rule is that there shall be sent out to their houses two quarts of barley-groats for each and half a pint of wine; but if they are present, they shall be given double shares of everything. They shall be honored in the same way when they have been invited to dinner by private persons. The kings, it is ordained, shall also have charge of the oracles given, but the Pythians too shall have knowledge of them. The rule is moreover that the kings alone give decision on the following cases only: about the maiden who inherits her father's property, namely who ought to have her if her father has not betrothed her to anyone, and about public ways; and if any man wishes to adopt a son, it must be done in the presence of the kings. It is ordained that they shall sit in council with the Senators, who are twenty-eight in number; and if they do not come, those of the Senators most closely related to them shall have the kings' privileges, and give two votes besides their own, making three in all.

The two men each Spartan king appoints to consult the god at Delphi, who eat at the public table with the kings and share the keeping of the oracles.

Thus are these things done; and at the time of which we speak, while Cleomenes was in Aegina doing deeds which were for the common service of Hellas, Demaratus was bringing charges against him—not so much because he cared about the Aeginetans as because he felt envy and jealousy of him. So Cleomenes, after he returned from Aegina, planned to depose Demaratus from the kingship, making an attempt upon him on the following grounds. For since she was ugly in appearance, her nurse, considering that she was the daughter of wealthy parents and was ill-favored in looks, and seeing moreover that her parents were distressed by it, devised the following plan. Every day she would carry her to the temple of Helen, which is at the place called Therapne, lying above the temple of Phoebus; and whenever the nurse carried her there, she would place her before the image and pray to the goddess to deliver the child from her ugliness. Once, as the nurse was leaving the temple, it is said that a woman appeared to her, and having appeared, asked what she was carrying in her arms; and she told her she was carrying a child. At this the other bade her show the child to her, but she refused, for she had been forbidden by the parents to show it to anyone; but the woman kept pressing her to show it. So, perceiving that the woman really wanted to see it, the nurse showed her the child. Then the woman stroked the child's head and said that she would be the fairest of all the women in Sparta; and from that day her appearance was changed. Afterwards, when she came of age, she was married to Agetus son of Alcides, this friend of Ariston of whom we spoke.

Ariston’s closest friend, who agreed to an exchange of any one possession, sworn on oath, and lost his wife by it.

## modern-en · menares · 951:0

Cleomenes, eager to take revenge on Demaratus, arranged matters with Leotychides, son of Menares, son of Agis — a man of the same royal house as Demaratus. The condition was this: if Leotychides were installed as king in Demaratus's place, he would join Cleomenes on the campaign against the Aeginetans. Leotychides already had reason enough to hate Demaratus, and the cause was as follows. Leotychides had been betrothed to Percalos, the daughter of Chilon son of Demarmenos. But Demaratus plotted against him and deprived him of the marriage, seizing Percalos himself beforehand and taking her for his own wife. This was the origin of the feud between Leotychides and Demaratus. And now, at Cleomenes's prompting, Leotychides stood up and swore an accusation against Demaratus, claiming that he had no right to the throne of Sparta because he was not truly the son of Ariston. After this formal charge he pressed his suit, recalling the old remark that Ariston had made when his servant came to announce that a son had been born to him: Ariston, counting up the months, had denied with an oath that the child was his. Leotychides seized on this utterance and argued that Demaratus was not Ariston's son and therefore had no right to rule Sparta. As witnesses he produced those Ephors who happened to have been sitting in council with Ariston at the time and had heard him say it.

Leotychides’s father.

## modern-en · cobon · 952:0

At last, since the dispute went on without resolution, the Spartans decided to send to Delphi and ask the oracle whether Demaratus was indeed the son of Ariston. The question was referred to the Pythian prophetess through Cleomenes's arrangement, and Cleomenes won over to his side Cobon son of Aristophantus, the most powerful man in Delphi. Cobon then persuaded Perialla, the prophetess of the oracle, to give the answer that Cleomenes wanted. So when the envoys arrived and put their question to the god, the Pythia declared that Demaratus was not the son of Ariston. Later, however, the whole business came to light: Cobon was driven into exile from Delphi, and Perialla was removed from her office as prophetess.

The most powerful man at Delphi, bought by Cleomenes to get the answer he wanted about Demaratus, and driven into exile when the business came out. The older translation spells him Cobon and Cobin in the same sentence.

Thus he spoke, and she answered him as follows: “My son, since you entreat me so earnestly to tell you the truth, the whole truth shall be told. When Ariston had brought me into his house, on the third night an apparition came to me in the likeness of Ariston; and after lying with me it placed upon me the garlands it was wearing and then went away. Soon afterward Ariston himself came. When he saw me wearing the garlands, he asked who had given them to me, and I said that he had. He denied it, but I began to swear to it, saying that he did wrong to deny it, for he had come only a short while before, lain with me, and given me the garlands. Then Ariston, seeing that I was taking an oath, realized that the matter was of the gods. And so indeed it was: the garlands were found to come from the hero-shrine that stands beside the outer door of our house — the shrine they call the temple of Astrabacus — and the diviners likewise answered that it was this very hero. So, my son, you now have the whole truth, as much as you wished to learn. You are begotten either of this hero — and Astrabacus is your father — or else of Ariston himself, for it was on that night that I conceived you. As for the point on which your enemies most eagerly seize — that Ariston, when your birth was announced, declared in the hearing of many that you were not his son, because the ten months had not yet been completed — he spoke that word out of ignorance of such matters. Women bring forth children at the ninth month as well, and even at the seventh, and not all after the full ten. I bore you, my son, at the seventh month; and Ariston himself before long recognized that he had uttered that saying in folly. Accept then no other reports about your birth; you have heard the entire truth. And as for Leotychides and all who spread such tales — may their own wives bear them children by keepers of asses!”

The hero of the shrine beside Ariston’s door, who Demaratus’s mother says came to her in her husband’s likeness and left his own garlands on her. The diviners agreed it was he.

When the Lacedaemonians learned what Cleomenes was up to, they grew afraid and proceeded to bring him back to Sparta to rule on the same terms as before. But no sooner had he returned than a madness seized him — he had never been entirely of sound mind — and whenever he met one of the Spartans on the street he would strike him in the face with his staff. As he kept doing this and had plainly lost his reason, his kinsmen bound him in stocks. While he was so bound, he noticed that his guard had been left alone by the others, and he asked him for a knife. At first the guard, a Helot, would not give it, but Cleomenes threatened him with what he would do afterwards if he refused, and at last the man was intimidated into handing it over. Then Cleomenes, once he had the blade, began to mutilate himself from the legs upward, slicing his flesh lengthways up from the legs to the thighs, from the thighs to the loins and flanks, until at last he reached his belly; cutting this into strips he died. Most of the Greeks say that this happened to him because he bribed the Pythian prophetess to give the answer she did about Demaratus. The Athenians alone say it was because, when he invaded Eleusis, he laid waste the sacred precinct of the Two Goddesses. The Argives say it was because he dragged out from their sanctuary of Argos those of their people who had fled there for refuge after the battle, slew them, and even set fire to the grove itself, thinking it of no account.

When the Aeginetans heard that Cleomenes was dead, they sent envoys to Sparta to denounce Leotychides for the business of the hostages being kept at Athens. There was much report of your uprightness throughout Greece, and especially in Ionia, and I reflected that Ionia is perpetually in danger, whereas the Peloponnese is secure, and that wealth rarely stays long with the same men. So, turning these things over in my mind, I decided to convert half of my property into silver and lodge it with you, well assured that if placed with you it would be safe. I beg you, therefore, take the money, and take these tokens and keep them; whoever asks for it back producing the matching tokens, to him return it.’ So spoke the stranger from Miletus, and Glaucus accepted the deposit on those terms. A long time passed, and the sons of the man who had made the deposit came to Sparta, spoke with Glaucus, and, producing the tokens, asked for the money to be returned. Glaucus turned them away, saying, ‘I do not remember the matter, nor can I recall anything of what you mention; but I want to think it over and do what is just. If I received it, I want to give it back honestly; if I did not, I will treat you according to the customs of the Greeks. I therefore defer settling the matter with you for three months from today.’ The Milesians went away in grief, thinking themselves cheated of the money. But Glaucus set out for Delphi to consult the oracle. When he asked the oracle whether he might seize the money by a false oath, the Pythia rebuked him in these lines:

The Lacedaemonian of two generations back whose honesty was a byword, and who asked Delphi whether he might keep a deposit by swearing falsely. The Pythia told him Oath has a son. He returned the money; there is not a descendant of his left in Sparta, nor a hearth reckoned as his.

So Hippias concluded that his dream had been thus fulfilled. Meanwhile the Athenians, drawn up in the sacred precinct of Heracles, were joined by the Plataeans, who came to their aid in full force. For the Plataeans had given themselves to the Athenians, and the Athenians had undertaken many labors on their behalf. The surrender had come about like this. Being oppressed by the Thebans, the Plataeans had first tried to give themselves to Cleomenes son of Anaxandridas and to the Lacedaemonians, who happened to be in the area. But the Lacedaemonians would not accept them and said: “We live too far off, and our help to you would be cold comfort. You might be enslaved many times over before any of us heard of it. We advise you instead to give yourselves to the Athenians — they are your neighbors, and they are no bad allies.” The Lacedaemonians gave this advice not so much out of goodwill for the Plataeans as out of a wish that the Athenians should be caught up in trouble and conflict with the Boeotians. The Plataeans did not fail to follow the counsel. While the Athenians were offering sacrifice to the twelve gods, the Plataeans seated themselves as suppliants at the altar and so handed themselves over. When the Thebans learned of this, they marched against the Plataeans, and the Athenians came to their defense. Just as the two sides were about to join battle, the Corinthians, who happened to be there, would not allow them to fight but reconciled the quarrel. Both parties put the matter in their hands, and the Corinthians fixed the boundaries of the land on the condition that the Thebans should leave alone any Boeotians who did not wish to be counted among them. After this decision the Corinthians departed. But as the Athenians were withdrawing, the Boeotians attacked them, and in the resulting battle were defeated. The Athenians then advanced beyond the boundaries the Corinthians had set for the Plataeans and made the river Asopus itself the border between Thebes and the territory of Plataea and Hysiae. The opinions of the Athenian generals were divided. One side argued that they should not fight a battle, since they were too few to engage the Median army; the other side, among them Miltiades, argued that they should. The worse opinion was on the point of prevailing. But since the man chosen by lot as polemarch of Athens had a vote in addition to the ten generals (for in those days the Athenians gave the polemarch an equal vote with the generals), and the polemarch at that time was Callimachus of the deme of Aphidnae, Miltiades came to him and said: “Callimachus, it rests with you now either to bring Athens into slavery, or to leave her free and so bequeath to all future generations a memorial even greater than Harmodius and Aristogiton left. For at this moment the Athenians face a greater danger than any they have faced since they became a people. If they submit to the Medes, it is already decided what they shall suffer, being handed over to Hippias; but if this city prevails, she may become the foremost of all the cities of Greece. How that may happen, and why the decision has fallen to you of all men, I shall now explain. Of us ten generals, the opinions are divided, some urging battle, some opposing it. If we do not fight, I expect some great spirit of discord will fall upon the Athenians and so shake them that they will go over to the Medes. But if we fight a battle before any rot can set in among the people, then — if the gods grant us a fair field — we can win. All of this now lies with you and depends on you. I was told that the story he used to tell about what had befallen him was this: that it seemed to him a tall man in full armor stood against him, whose beard cast a shadow across his whole shield; that this apparition passed him by, but killed the man standing next to him. The one Athenian who dared buy Peisistratus’s goods at auction when he was driven out, and devised every other hostility he could against him. He won the horse race at Olympia and was second in the chariot, and he let each of his three daughters marry the man in Athens she chose.

## modern-en · megacles-elder · 1011:0

Now the family of the Alcmaeonidae had already been prominent at Athens from the earliest times, and they became very greatly distinguished from the time of Alcmaeon and of Megacles after him. For Alcmaeon son of Megacles made himself of use to the Lydians sent from Croesus at Sardis to the oracle at Delphi, and assisted them energetically. When Croesus heard from the Lydians who had gone to the oracle that this man had served him well, he summoned him to Sardis, and when he arrived Croesus offered him as a gift as much gold as he could carry away on his own person at one time. With such a gift in view, Alcmaeon made preparations and resorted to these devices. He put on a large tunic, letting a deep fold of it hang open at the front, and he pulled on the widest boots he could find. So equipped he went into the treasury to which they led him. There he threw himself onto a heap of gold dust, and first he packed along the sides of his legs as much gold as his boots would hold; then he filled the whole fold of his tunic with gold and sprinkled some of the gold dust on his hair and took some into his mouth. Having done this, he came out of the treasury, dragging his boots with difficulty and looking like anything on earth except a man — for his mouth was stuffed full and every part of him was bulging. Croesus burst out laughing when he saw him, and not only gave him everything he was carrying but presented him with even more besides, of no less value. So this family became enormously wealthy, and this same Alcmaeon of whom I speak became a breeder of chariot horses and won a victory at Olympia.

Alcmaeon’s father, at the head of the Alcmaeonid line.

## modern-en · aristonymus · 1012:0

Then in the next generation after this, Cleisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon raised the family still higher, so that it became much more famous among the Greeks than before. Cleisthenes son of Aristonymus, son of Myron, son of Andreas, had a daughter named Agariste, and he made it his purpose to find the best man in Greece and marry her to him. So when the Olympic games were being held and Cleisthenes won them with a four-horse chariot, he had it proclaimed that any Greek who considered himself worthy to be Cleisthenes's son-in-law should come to Sicyon by the sixtieth day, or sooner if he wished, for Cleisthenes meant to conclude the marriage within a year, counting from that sixtieth day. All those Greeks who took pride either in themselves or in their high birth came as suitors, and for them Cleisthenes had built a running-track and a wrestling-ground kept expressly for their use.

Cleisthenes of Sicyon’s father.

From Italy came Smindyrides son of Hippocrates of Sybaris, who of all men on earth had attained the highest degree of luxury (for Sybaris was at that time at the height of its prosperity), and Damasus of Siris, son of that Amyris who was called the Wise; these came from Italy. From the Ionian gulf came Amphimnestus son of Epistrophus of Epidamnus; from Aetolia came Males, the brother of that Titormus who surpassed all Greeks in strength and who fled the company of men to the remotest part of the Aetolian land. From the Peloponnese came Leocedes son of Pheidon the tyrant of the Argives — the Pheidon who established the standard weights and measures still used in the Peloponnese, and who outdid all other Greeks in outrageous arrogance, for he removed the Elean presidents of the games from their posts and presided over the Olympic games himself; I say, his son, and with him Amiantus son of Lycurgus, an Arcadian from Trapezus; and Laphanes, an Azanian from the city of Paios, the son of that Euphorion who, according to the Arcadian story, entertained the Dioscuri in his home and from then on made a point of welcoming everyone who came; and Onomastus son of Agaios of Elis — these came from the Peloponnese itself. From Athens came Megacles, son of that Alcmaeon who had gone to Croesus, and with him Hippocleides son of Tisander, who surpassed the other Athenians in both wealth and good looks. From Eretria, which was then flourishing, came Lysanias, alone from Euboea. From Thessaly came Diactorides of Crannon, a member of the Scopad family; and from the Molossians, Alcon.

From the Peloponnese came Leocedes son of Pheidon the tyrant of the Argives — the Pheidon who established the standard weights and measures still used in the Peloponnese, and who outdid all other Greeks in outrageous arrogance, for he removed the Elean presidents of the games from their posts and presided over the Olympic games himself; I say, his son, and with him Amiantus son of Lycurgus, an Arcadian from Trapezus; and Laphanes, an Azanian from the city of Paios, the son of that Euphorion who, according to the Arcadian story, entertained the Dioscuri in his home and from then on made a point of welcoming everyone who came; and Onomastus son of Agaios of Elis — these came from the Peloponnese itself. From Athens came Megacles, son of that Alcmaeon who had gone to Croesus, and with him Hippocleides son of Tisander, who surpassed the other Athenians in both wealth and good looks. From Eretria, which was then flourishing, came Lysanias, alone from Euboea. From Thessaly came Diactorides of Crannon, a member of the Scopad family; and from the Molossians, Alcon.

An Arcadian suitor, from Trapezus.

## modern-en · molossians · 145:0

For this reason, then, the Ionians also made twelve cities for themselves; for to say that these are in any way more Ionian than the other Ionians, or have a nobler descent, is mere folly. A large part of them are Abantians from Euboea, who have no share even in the name of Ionia; Minyai of Orchomenos have been mingled with them; also Cadmeians, Dryopians, Phokians who seceded from their native state, Molossians, Pelasgians of Arcadia, Dorians of Epidauros, and many other races have been mingled with them. And those of them who set forth to their settlements from the City Hall of Athens, and who consider themselves the most nobly born of the Ionians — these, I say, brought no women with them to their settlement, but took Carian women, whose parents they slew. On account of this slaughter, these women laid down a rule for themselves, imposing oaths on one another and handing it down to their daughters, that they should never eat with their husbands, nor should a wife call her own husband by name. This was because the Ionians had slain their fathers and husbands and children, and then, having done this, had taken them as wives. This happened at Miletos.

The people Alcon came from.

## modern-en · lysagoras · 1019:0

Having taken command of the force, Miltiades sailed against Paros, under the pretext that the Parians had first attacked Athens by sending triremes to Marathon along with the Persians — this was the excuse he put forward publicly, but he also had a private grudge against the Parians on account of Lysagoras son of Tisias, a Parian by birth, who had denounced him to Hydarnes the Persian. So when Miltiades arrived at his destination, he laid siege to the Parians with his army, first shutting them up within their walls; and sending a herald in to them he demanded one hundred talents, saying that if they refused to pay, his army would not withdraw until it had conquered them completely. The Parians had no intention of giving Miltiades any money; they thought only of how they might defend their city, and among many other contrivances they adopted this one: wherever at any point the wall was exposed to attack, they raised it to double its height under cover of night.

The Parian who denounced Miltiades to Hydarnes the Persian, and so gave him a private grudge against Paros to go with the public one.

## modern-en · timo · 1020:0

So much of the story is told by all the Greeks; but what followed the Parians alone report, and they say it happened like this. Miltiades, they say, was at a loss, when a woman came to speak with him, a Parian by birth named Timo who had been taken prisoner; she was an under-priestess of the chthonic goddesses. Coming into Miltiades's presence, she advised him that if it was of great importance to him to take Paros, he should do what she was about to suggest, and then she told him her meaning. So he crossed over to the hill that lies in front of the city and leapt over the fence of the temple of Demeter the Lawgiver, since he could not open the door; and having got over the fence, he went on towards the inner sanctuary, intending to do something inside — whether to lay hands on something that should not be touched, or whatever else he had in mind. When he reached the door, a sudden shuddering dread came over him and he set off to go back the way he had come; and as he leapt down from the wall of rough stones, his thigh was dislocated, or, as others say, he struck his knee against the wall.

The Parian under-priestess of the chthonic goddesses, a prisoner, who told Miltiades what to do to take Paros. The Parians wanted to kill her for it; the Pythia would not allow it, since Timo was not the author of the business but the means by which a man fated to end badly was led to his end.
