## modern-en · harmokydes · 1420:0

While Mardonius was encamped in Boeotia, the rest of the Greeks who lived in these parts and took the Medes' side were all supplying troops and had joined in the invasion of Attica. Only the Phokians had not joined in the invasion — the Phokians, I say, for they too were now actively taking the side of the Medes, not of their own will but under compulsion. Not many days after Mardonius's arrival at Thebes, a thousand of their hoplites came, led by Harmokydes, the man of greatest repute among their citizens. When these too came to Thebes, Mardonius sent horsemen and bade the Phokians take up position by themselves in the plain. After they had done so, the whole cavalry suddenly appeared, and a rumor spread through the Greek army on the Median side that the cavalry was about to shoot them down with javelins; this same report went through the Phokians themselves. Then their commander Harmokydes exhorted them as follows: “Phokians, it is clear that these men mean to deliver us to an easily foreseen death, because we have been falsely accused by the Thessalians, I conjecture. Now, therefore, it is right that every one of you prove himself a good man, for it is better to end our lives performing deeds of valor and defending ourselves than to be destroyed by a dishonorable death as offered victims. Let each of them learn that they are barbarians, and we — against whom they devised murder — are Greeks.”

The man of greatest repute among the Phocians, who brought their thousand hoplites to Thebes; and when Mardonius’s whole cavalry closed on them with missiles already levelled, told them it was better to end their lives performing deeds of valour than to be destroyed like offered victims. They closed ranks, and the horsemen turned and rode back.

## modern-en · echemos · 1429:0

Then, in the arranging of the various posts, there arose much heated argument between the Tegeans and the Athenians, for each claimed to occupy the other wing of the army themselves, citing deeds both new and old. The Tegeans said: “We have always been judged worthy of this post by the whole body of allies in every joint expedition the Peloponnesians have made, whether long ago or recently, ever since the time when the sons of Heracles tried, after the death of Eurystheus, to return to the Peloponnese. We gained this honor then because of this event: when we, with the Achaians and the Ionians then in the Peloponnese, had come out to the Isthmus to help and were encamped opposite those wishing to return, Hyllos is said to have proposed that it was not right for one army to risk its safety in battle with the other, and urged instead that the man whom the Peloponnesian army judged to be the best of them should fight Hyllos himself in single combat on terms agreed between them. The Peloponnesians resolved that this should be done, and they swore an oath together on this condition: if Hyllos conquered the Peloponnesians' chosen man, then the sons of Heracles should return to their father's inheritance; but if he were conquered, then the sons of Heracles should depart and lead away their army and not try for a hundred years to return to the Peloponnese. Of all the allies there was chosen — he himself making a voluntary offer — Echemos son of Aëropos son of Phegeus, who was our commander and king. He fought a single combat and killed Hyllos. Because of this deed, we obtained among the Peloponnesians of that time — besides many other great privileges we still possess — this one too: always leading the other wing of the army whenever a joint expedition is made. To you Lacedaemonians we offer no opposition, and we give you the choice of whichever wing you wish to command; but of the other, we say, it belongs to us to lead, as in former times. And apart from this deed just related, we are worthier than the Athenians to hold this post, for we have fought many glorious contests against you, Spartans, and many against others too. So it is just that we have the other wing rather than the Athenians, since they have performed no such deeds as ours, old or new.”

Aëropus’s son and Phegeus’s grandson, the Tegeans’ commander and king, who made a voluntary offer of himself for the single combat at the Isthmus and killed Hyllus — the deed for which, the Tegeans said at Plataea, they had led the other wing ever since.

It happened by chance that the Megarians were posted in the most assailable part of the whole position, where the cavalry could best approach. ## modern-en · tisamenus-diviner · 1436:0

When all had been drawn up by nations and divisions, on the next day they offered sacrifice on both sides. For the Greeks, Tisamenos son of Antiochos was the one who sacrificed, since he accompanied the army as diviner. This man the Lacedaemonians had made one of their own citizens, being an Eleian of the race of the Iamidai. For when Tisamenos was seeking divination at Delphi concerning issue, the Pythian priestess answered him that he should win five of the greatest contests. Missing the oracle's meaning, he turned to athletic games, supposing he would win athletic contests; he practiced for the pentathlon and came within a single fall of winning an Olympic victory, being matched against Hieronymos of Andros. But the Lacedaemonians perceived that the oracle given to Tisamenos referred not to athletic but to martial contests, and they tried to persuade Tisamenos by payment of money to become a leader in their wars alongside the kings of the house of Heracles. He, seeing that the Spartans set much store on gaining him as a friend, raised his price and made clear that he would do what they wanted only if they made him a citizen of their state with full rights — but for no other payment. At first the Spartans, hearing this, displayed indignation and gave up their request altogether; but at last, when great fear of this Persian armament hung over them, they gave in and agreed. He, perceiving they had changed their minds, then said that even so he could not now be satisfied with these terms alone: it was also necessary that his brother Hegias be made a Spartan citizen on the same terms as himself.

Antiochus’s son, an Elean of the Iamidae, told at Delphi that he would win five of the greatest contests. Taking it for athletics he trained for the pentathlon and came within one fall of an Olympic crown; the Lacedaemonians worked out that the oracle meant wars, and he held out against every payment until they made him a Spartan citizen with full rights — and then raised the price again and made them do the same for his brother Hegias. Plataea was the first of his five.

## modern-en · hegesistratus-elis · 1440:0

Mardonius too, eager to begin a battle, found the sacrifices unfavorable for that purpose, though they were of good omen for him if he merely defended himself; for he too used the Greek manner of sacrifice, having as diviner Hegesistratos, an Eleian and the most famous of the Telliadai. Before these events the Spartans had captured and bound him, intending to put him to death for the much mischief they had suffered from him. In this evil state, seeing that he was running for his life and was likely to suffer much torment before death, he did a deed that is scarcely credible. Being fastened on a block bound with iron, he obtained an iron tool that had somehow been brought in, and at once devised a feat as courageous as any we know: for having first calculated how the remaining part of his foot might be freed from the block, he cut off the flat of his own foot. After that, since he was still guarded by warders, he broke through the wall and ran off to Tegea, traveling during the nights and in daytime entering a wood and resting there. Although the Lacedaemonians searched for him in full force, he reached Tegea on the third night. The Lacedaemonians were struck with great wonder both at his courage (when they saw the severed piece of foot lying there) and at their inability to find him. So he escaped them then, taking refuge at Tegea, which at that time was not friendly with the Lacedaemonians. Once healed, and having procured a wooden foot for himself, he became an open enemy of the Lacedaemonians. In the end, however, the enmity he had fallen into with the Lacedaemonians was not to his advantage; for he was caught by them while practicing divination in Zakynthos and was put to death.

An Elean and the most famous of the Telliadae, hired by Mardonius at no small price. The Spartans had once had him fastened in an iron-bound block to be put to death for the mischief he had done them; he calculated how much of his own foot would have to go, cut off the flat of it, broke through the wall, and travelled to Tegea in three nights, resting in a wood by day. They found the piece of foot and never found him. He got himself a wooden one and was their open enemy until they caught him practising divination in Zacynthus and killed him — later than Plataea.

Among the barbarians, those who proved themselves the best men were, of the foot, the Persians, and of the cavalry, the Sacans; and for a single man, Mardonius, it is said, was the best. Of the Greeks, though both Tegeans and Athenians proved themselves good men, the Lacedaemonians surpassed them in valor. Of this I have no other proof (for all these were victorious over their opposite numbers), except this: that they fought the strongest part of the enemy's force and overcame it. The man who, in my opinion, by far proved himself the best was that Aristodemos who, having come back alone of the three hundred safely from Thermopylae, had reproach and dishonor attached to him. This, however, they perhaps said out of ill will. ## modern-en · hegetorides · 1479:0

When the barbarians had been laid low by the Greeks at Plataea, a woman approached — the concubine of Pharandates son of Teaspis, a Persian — coming over of her own free will from the enemy. When she perceived that the Persians had been destroyed and that the Greeks were victorious, she descended from her carriage and came up to the Lacedaemonians while they were still engaged in the slaughter. She had adorned herself with many gold ornaments, and her attendants likewise, and she had put on the finest of her robes. Seeing that Pausanias was directing everything there — being already familiar with his name and lineage, which she had heard often — she recognized Pausanias, took hold of his knees, and said: “O king of Sparta, deliver your suppliant from the slavery of the captive. For you have already done me a service by destroying these men, who have respect for neither demigods nor gods. I am by race of Cos, the daughter of Hegetorides son of Antagoras; and the Persian took me by force in Cos and kept me a prisoner.” He answered: “Woman, be of good courage — both because you are a suppliant, and also, if in addition it chances that you are speaking the truth and are the daughter of Hegetorides of Cos, who is bound to me as guest-friend more than any other man dwelling in those parts.” Having said this, he for the time put her in charge of the Ephors present; and afterwards he sent her to Aegina, where she herself wished to go.

Of Cos, Antagoras’s son, bound to Pausanias as guest-friend more than any other man in those parts — which is why his daughter, taken by force in Cos and kept a prisoner, was safe the moment she said his name.

Now do also what remains to be done after this, so that yet greater reputation may attach to you, and that in future every barbarian may beware of being the first to commit outrageous deeds against Greeks. ## modern-en · cleades · 1488:0

He was buried, then, in some such manner. The Greeks, having divided the spoils at Plataea, proceeded to bury their dead, each nation apart. The Spartans made themselves three separate burial-places: in one they buried the younger Spartans, among whom were Poseidonios, Amompharetos, Philokyon, and Callicrates; in the second, the rest of the Spartans; in the third, the Helots. They then buried their dead thus. The Tegeans buried theirs together in a place apart from these; the Athenians, theirs together; the Megarians and Phliasians, those who had been killed by the cavalry. The burial-places of all these contained bodies; but as for the burial-places of other cities to be seen at Plataea, these, as I am told, are all merely mounds of earth without bodies in them, raised by the various peoples on account of posterity, because they were ashamed of their absence from the fight. Among others there is one called the burial-place of the Aeginetans, which I hear was raised at the request of the Aeginetans by Cleades son of Autodicos, a Plataean who was their public guest-friend, no less than ten years after these events.

Autodicus’s son, a Plataean and the Aeginetans’ public guest-friend, who raised their empty burial-mound at Plataea for them no less than ten years after the battle.

## modern-en · dekelos · 1476:0

Of the Athenians, the man who gained most glory is said to have been Sophanes son of Eutychides of the deme of Dekeleia — a deme whose inhabitants long ago performed a deed that has been of service to them ever since, as the Athenians themselves report. For when, in olden times, the sons of Tyndareus invaded Attica with a great army to bring back Helen, and were laying waste the demes — not knowing to what hiding place Helen had been taken — then they say that the men of Dekeleia (or, as some say, Dekelos himself), aggrieved by the insolence of Theseus and fearing for the whole land of the Athenians, told them the whole matter and led them to Aphidnai, which Titakos, a man sprung from the soil, delivered up by treachery to the sons of Tyndareus. As a result of this deed, the Dekeleians have continued to enjoy freedom from dues at Sparta and front seats at the games — privileges still in effect to this day. Indeed, in the war which arose many years after these events between the Athenians and Peloponnesians, when the Lacedaemonians laid waste all the rest of Attica, they spared Dekeleia from harm.

The man of Deceleia — or, as some say, the deme itself — who was aggrieved at Theseus’s insolence, feared for the whole land of the Athenians, and told the sons of Tyndareus where Helen was hidden.

When these were brought before the commanders, Hegesistratos spoke at length using all kinds of arguments, saying that as soon as the Ionians saw them, they would at once revolt from the Persians, and that the barbarians would not await the attack; and if after all they did, the Greeks would take a prize such as they would never take again thereafter. Appealing to the gods worshipped in common, he tried to persuade them to rescue men who were Greeks from slavery and to drive the barbarian away. This was easy for them to do, he said, because the enemy's ships sailed badly and were no match for theirs in battle. Moreover, if the Greeks suspected they were trying to lead them on by fraud, the envoys were ready to be taken as hostages in their ships.

Athenagoras’s father.

Beside these were drawn up a thousand Troizenians; next to the Troizenians, two hundred Lepreates; next, four hundred men of Mykene and Tiryns; then a thousand Phliasians. Beside these stood three hundred Hermionians; next to the Hermionians were posted six hundred Eretrians and Styrians; next to these, four hundred Chalcidians; and then five hundred men of Amprakia. After these stood eight hundred Leucadians and Anactorians; next to them, two hundred from Pale in Cephallenia. After these were arrayed five hundred Aeginetans; beside them, three thousand Megarians; and next to these, six hundred Plataeans. Last — or, if you prefer, first — were arrayed the Athenians, holding the left wing, eight thousand in number, and their commander was Aristides son of Lysimachos.

Who stood with the Leucadians at Plataea, eight hundred between them.

## modern-en · palians · 1434:0

Meanwhile, Mardonius's barbarians, when they had sufficiently mourned for Masistios and were informed that the Greeks were at Plataea, themselves came to that part of the Asopos which flows there. Once arrived, Mardonius ranged them against the enemy as follows: against the Lacedaemonians he stationed the Persians; and since the Persians much outnumbered the Lacedaemonians, he arrayed them in deeper ranks, and even so they extended in front of the Tegeans as well. He arranged them in this way: all the strongest part of that body he picked out from the rest and posted opposite the Lacedaemonians, and the weaker part he ranged beside them, opposite the Tegeans. This he did on the information and suggestion of the Thebans. Next to the Persians he placed the Medes, who extended in front of the Corinthians, Potidaians, Orchomenians, and Sikyonians. Next to the Medes he ranged the Bactrians, who extended in front of the Epidaurians, Troizenians, Lepreates, Tirynthians, Myceneans, and Phliasians. After the Bactrians he posted the Indians, who extended in front of the Hermionians, Eretrians, Styrians, and Chalcidians. Next to the Indians he placed the Sacans, extending in front of the men of Amprakia, Anactorians, Leucadians, Palians, and Aeginetans. Next to the Sacans, and opposite the Athenians, Plataeans, and Megarians, he stationed the Boeotians, Locrians, Malians, Thessalians, and the thousand men of the Phokians: for not all the Phokians had taken the side of the Medes — some were even supporting the Greek cause, being shut up on Parnassos, and setting out from there they plundered from the army of Mardonius and those Greeks with him. He ranged the Macedonians, too, and those dwelling around the borders of Thessaly opposite the Athenians.

The men of Pale in Cephallenia, two hundred of them, ranged opposite the Sacae.

## modern-en · mycenaeans · 1430:0

So they spoke, and the Athenians replied: “Though we know this gathering was assembled for battle with the barbarian and not for speeches, yet since the Tegean has set us the task of speaking of things both old and new — the deeds of merit achieved by each of our two nations through all time — we must point out to you from what source it is that we, who have always been brave men, have the chief place as a heritage rather than the Arcadians. First, as to the sons of Heracles — whose leader they claim to have killed at the Isthmus — in earlier times, when they were being driven away by all the Greeks to whom they had fled to escape slavery under the Myceneans, we alone received them, and joining with them we subdued the insolence of Eurystheus, defeating in battle those who then dwelt in the Peloponnese. Again, when the Argives who marched with Polyneikes against Thebes had been killed and lay unburied, we declare that we marched an army against the Cadmeians and recovered the dead bodies, burying them in our own land at Eleusis. We have another glorious deed performed against the Amazons who once invaded Attica from the river Thermodon. And in the toils of Troy we were inferior to none. But it is no use making mention of these things — for though we were brave men then, we might by now have become worthless; or though we were worthless then, we might be better now. Let what concerns ancient deeds suffice. But even if we had displayed no other deed (though many glorious ones there are, no fewer than any other Greek people's), by reason of the deed accomplished at Marathon alone we are worthy to have this privilege, and others besides — for we alone of all the Greeks fought in single combat with the Persian, and having undertaken so great a task, we overcame and defeated forty-six nations. Are we not worthy, then, to hold this post on that deed alone? However, since at such a time as this it is not fitting to contend for a post, we are ready to follow what you say, Lacedaemonians, as to where you think it most suitable for us to stand and against whom; for wherever we are posted, we shall try to be brave men. Prescribe to us, then, and we shall obey.” Thus they answered; and the whole body of Lacedaemonians shouted aloud that the Athenians were more worthy to hold the wing than the Arcadians. So the Athenians got the wing and overcame the Tegeans.

Of Mycenae, counted with the Tirynthians at Plataea; and, the Athenians say, the people whose slavery the sons of Heracles were fleeing when all the Greeks but Athens turned them away.

## modern-en · cadmeians · 145:0

For this reason, then, the Ionians also made twelve cities for themselves; for to say that these are in any way more Ionian than the other Ionians, or have a nobler descent, is mere folly. A large part of them are Abantians from Euboea, who have no share even in the name of Ionia; Minyai of Orchomenos have been mingled with them; also Cadmeians, Dryopians, Phokians who seceded from their native state, Molossians, Pelasgians of Arcadia, Dorians of Epidauros, and many other races have been mingled with them. And those of them who set forth to their settlements from the City Hall of Athens, and who consider themselves the most nobly born of the Ionians — these, I say, brought no women with them to their settlement, but took Carian women, whose parents they slew. On account of this slaughter, these women laid down a rule for themselves, imposing oaths on one another and handing it down to their daughters, that they should never eat with their husbands, nor should a wife call her own husband by name. This was because the Ionians had slain their fathers and husbands and children, and then, having done this, had taken them as wives. This happened at Miletos.

The old people of Thebes. Some of them were mixed into Ionia; they were driven out by the Argives in Laodamas’s reign and went off to the Enchelians, leaving the Gephyraeans behind; and the Athenians say they marched against them to recover the Argive dead who lay unburied under the walls.

## modern-en · enchelians · 822:2

It was in the reign of this very Laodamas, son of Eteocles, that the Cadmeians were driven out by the Argives and went off to join the Encheleans; and the Gephyraeans, left behind then, were afterwards forced by the Boeotians to withdraw to Athens. Moreover, they have temples established in Athens in which the other Athenians have no part; and among other distinctive shrines, they have especially a temple of Demeter Achaia and a celebration of her mysteries.

To whom the Cadmeians went when the Argives drove them out — and whose army, Herodotus says, the oracle Mardonius took for a Persian one was actually composed about, along with the Illyrians.

## modern-en · messenians · 444:0

Then the Lacedemonians prepared a force and made an expedition to Samos, in repayment of former services, as the Samians say, because the Samians had first helped them with ships against the Messenians. But the Lacedemonians say they made the expedition not so much from a desire to help the Samians at their request, as to take vengeance on their own behalf for the robbery of the mixing-bowl they had been carrying as a gift to Croesus, and of the corslet which Amasis, king of Egypt, had sent as a gift to them; for the Samians had carried off the corslet as well, in the year before they took the bowl. The corslet was of linen with many figures woven into it and embroidered with gold and cotton, and each thread of this corslet is worthy of admiration, for though it is itself fine, it has in it three hundred and sixty fibers, all plainly visible. Another such as this, moreover, is the one Amasis dedicated as an offering to Athene at Lindos.

Against whom the Samians say they helped Sparta with ships, and whom a Spartan king was once told not to risk battles against for the sake of foreigners. A Messenian named Panites told the Spartans how to find out which of Aristodemus’s twins was the elder; one of Tisamenus’s five contests was fought against them at Ithome; and Arimnestus died at Stenyclerus taking three hundred men against their whole army.
